    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) After entering Mathura, Krishna was worshipped by the florist Sudama and the maiden Trivakra (Kubja). The elephant Kuvalayapida, however, challenged Him and was comfortably dispatched, after which Krishna killed the two wrestlers and King Kamsa. After completing Their studies at gurukula , Krishna and Balarama brought back Sandipani Muni’s dead son. While in Mathura, Krishna (through Uddhava) sent a message to the gopis , visited Trivakra’s house, defeated Jarasandha seventeen times, and favoured Mucukunda by appearing before him in a cave.

    Cry for Krishna

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Cry for Krishna “Sri Uddhava is described in this verse as buddhi-sattamah, “the most intelligent,” and thus he could expertly pacify the residents of Vrindavana, who were feeling such intense separation from Lord Krishna. Then, upon his return to Mathura, Uddhava would describe to all the members of the Vrsni dynasty the extraordinary pure love he had seen in Vrindavana. Indeed, the love the cowherd men and gopis felt for Krishna was far beyond anything the Lord’s other devotees had ever experienced, and by hearing about that love all the Lord’s devotees would increase their faith and devotion.” ( SB 10.46.1 ) Srila Visvanatha Chakravarti Thakura explains how one can place valuable gold within a fire to ascertain its purity. In the same way, he says, Krishna placed His most beloved devotees, the residents of Vrindavana, in the fire of separation from Him, just to reveal the purity of their love. From the day Krishna left Vrindavana, Mother Yasoda could only see His beautiful face, and she cried constantly despite being consoled by friends and family. When Uddhava came, she was so overwhelmed by love that she couldn’t even interact with him. These were the unique manifestations of love in separation that Krishna wanted Uddhava to witness. Interestingly, Krishna Himself came to this world to experience those same emotions. Krishna is known as rasaraja , the king of all relationships. As the fierce Nrsinghadeva, He savoured the mood of servitude that His devotees embody. As Lord Ramachandra, He experienced the brotherly love of Laksman and marital joy with Sita. As Lord Krishna, He relished intimate friendship with the cowherd boys, and unwedded paramour love with the cowherd girls. Although Krishna delighted in these relationships, a curiosity still remained. Krishna had not yet experienced the spiritual emotion that His devotees feel in their relationship with Him. It is said that Srimati Radharani, the most celebrated devotee, feels pleasure which is ten million times greater than the Lord’s! Thus, Sri Chaitanya, the manifestation of Krishna in Kali-yuga, descended to:

    Delight in the position of Srimati Radharani

    Understand the sweetness of Krishna’s qualities

    Experience the happiness of a pure devotee

    As the ‘maintainer’ of the universe, Visvambhara (Sri Chaitanya) taught the world what life’s priority really is. Though maintenance of the body is essential, one should not forget the necessity of the soul: to reawaken pure love of God ( prayojana ). The great teacher Visvanatha Chakravarti Thakura summarises the four main precepts that Sri Chaitanya came to teach: 1) The Goal: Pure Love of God The essence of each spirit soul is to seek love and express love. We spend our lives looking for those persons and objects in which we can repose the loving sentiment, but we’re often left frustrated and dissatisfied. When we develop our love for Krishna, however, we not only feel deep fulfillment and satisfaction, but we connect with others on a much deeper and satisfying level as well. By loving Krishna we become a conduit of love for others. 2) The Object of Love: Sri Krishna (who resides in Vrindavana) In Sanskrit, God is known as ‘Bhagavan,’ or the possessor of all opulences. Jiva Goswami explains that God is more intimately known as Krishna, and Bhagavan stands for bhajaniya guna visistha: “One whose qualities are so enchanting that nobody can resist worshipping Him.” Only Sri Krishna manifests the glories of God in full. Krishna, whose eternal playground is Vrindavana, performs exquisite pastimes of love there, and never takes one step out of that sacred land. Even when it appears that He has left, He remains there in a concealed form. 3) The Example of Love: Gopis of Vrindavana Amongst Vrindavana’s residents, the love of the gopis is particularly special since they sacrificed everything to be with Krishna. They left their family members, disregarded social customs, rejected the path of chastity and underwent all tribulations to be with Him. They were unconcerned with people’s opinions, and held nothing back, exhibiting affection without constraint. After meeting with the gopis , Krishna apparently left Vrindavana, throwing the cowherd maidens into an intense love in separation known as vipralambha-bhava. Their feelings of transcendental madness are considered the highest expressions of the soul in connection with God. 4) The Guidebook for Developing Love: Srimad-Bhagavatam Though such ecstatic emotions seem far and distant for the conditioned soul, the Srimad-Bhagavatam is the priceless guidebook to help us reawaken that love. It describes the incredible feelings of the most celebrated devotees in creation, but also narrates historical incidents and didactic passages which help one progress to such pure devotion. Thus, the light of Srimad-Bhagavatam is an incredible blend of inspiration and instruction for the lost souls in this dark age of Kali-yuga.

    Separation for a Sadhaka

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Cry for Krishna Separation for a Sadhaka The mood of separation from Krishna is not only an intensified emotional state found in pure devotees, but is also a cultivation that can assist the practitioner devotees in their spiritual progress. In 1969, Srila Prabhupada instructed the devotees to cry prayerfully for Krishna while chanting His name: “So we are addressing, Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna: ’O the energy of the Lord, O the Lord, please accept me.’ That’s all. ’Please accept me.’ We have no other prayer. ’Please accept me.’ Lord Chaitanya taught that we should simply cry, and we shall simply pray for accepting us. That’s all. So this vibration is simply a cry for addressing the Supreme Lord, requesting Him, ’Please accept me. Please accept me.’” Srila Prabhupada confirms this in another place: “This crying is the last word in the progressive path of devotional service. One who can cry for the Lord in love is certainly successful in the line of devotional service.” (SB 3.4.35) It is said that separation is the best mood in which to perform one’s spiritual practices. When we are chanting Hare Krishna with an awareness of how we separated from Krishna, we’ll begin to feel a deep necessity to reconnect with Him. Srila Prabhupada once said, “Actually, meeting Krishna is possible through the attitude of separation taught by Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. When the feeling of separation becomes very intense, one attains the stage of meeting Sri Krishna.” ( CC Adi 4.108 ) The acaryas explain that vipralambha , love in separation, expresses itself in four varieties: Purva-raga – the feeling of separation that is experienced before the lovers actually meet and express their sentiments for one another Mana – the feeling of separation that is experienced when lovers quarrel with one another Prema-vaicittya – the feeling of separation that occurs when the lovers are together but they fear the potentiality of parting Pravasa – the feeling of separation that occurs when lovers are actually parted by distance and time In analysing the relevance of these for a practitioner devotee ( sadhaka ), Bhaktivinoda Thakura comments as follows: “It is essential for the sadhaka jivas to cultivate only the mood of vipralambha , and because they have never experienced meeting with Krishna, their vipralambha will come only in the category of purva-raga. But without having ever met with Krishna, how can they experience separation in purva-raga from Him? By hearing the lila-katha of Sri Krishna from others, purva-raga is awakened. This was the case with the dvija-patnis as well as the ladies of Mathura before Krishna’s arrival there. Rukmini also had never seen Krishna, but by hearing about Him from Sri Narada, purva-raga arose within her heart. Thus she became exceedingly anxious to meet with Krishna. Similarly, by hearing from the guru and Vaisnavas or by reading the sastras , the jivas may have purva-raga vipralambha awakened within their hearts.”

    The Mood of Sri Chaitanya

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Cry for Krishna The Mood of Sri Chaitanya For the final twelve years of Sri Chaitanya’s manifest pastimes, He remained secluded in the Gambhira, the garden house of Kasi Misra. The Lord merged into a deep spiritual communion, obsessed day and night in thought of Krishna. This esoteric phenomenon is described by Krishnadasa Kaviraja Goswami: “When Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu felt separation from Krishna, His condition exactly corresponded to that of the gopis in Vrindavana after Krishna’s departure for Mathura. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s emotions exactly corresponded to those of Srimati Radharani when She met Uddhava in Vrindavana.” Sri Chaitanya’s ecstasy resulted in bodily transformations and delirious behaviour which resembled that of a madman. He would sometimes catch hold of the necks of His associates and plead “My dear friends, please listen to Me. What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where can I go to get Krishna? Please, both of you, tell Me how I can find Him.” In this way, Sri Chaitanya exhibited the intense longing of a pure devotee.

    Dwaraka Established

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Dwaraka Established Chapter 50, 51 When Kamsa’s two wives complained to their father, Jarasandha, about their husband’s death, Jarasandha decided to attack Krishna. The brothers annihilated his armies, and when Balarama was poised to arrest Jarasandha, Krishna decided to set him free. Krishna wanted Jarasandha to attack multiple times since it would facilitate a large-scale annihilation of his demoniac forces. In total, Jarasandha’s armies were defeated seventeen times. During the eighteenth attack, Narada Muni instigated the wicked Kalayavana and his 30 million soldiers to also join in. The dual attack tipped the scales, and Krishna thus created a magnificent city in the sea (Dwaraka), and mystically transferred the entire Yadava clan there for safety. When Kalayavana pursued Krishna to kill Him, he was led into a mountain cave. In that dark cave, Kalayavana kicked a man he thought was Krishna. That personality stood up and burned Kalayavana to death! This was Mucukunda, who had been awarded the boon of unbroken sleep, and also the power to annihilate anyone who interrupted it. After seeing the beautiful form of Krishna, Mucukunda lamented his absorption in material affairs, and thus requested the divine gift of pure devotional service.

    Gurukula

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Gurukula Chapter 45 Krishna consoled Vasudeva and Devaki for the traumatic incidents they had to endure, and expressed His indebtedness for each of their incredible sacrifices. After reinstating Ugrasena on the throne, many exiled family members returned and everyone felt safe and secure again. Krishna bade farewell to Nanda Maharaja, who returned to Vrindavana with all the cowherd community. To set the ideal example, Krishna and Balarama then took their vows of brahmacarya and began their education in Avantipura, at the school of Sandipani Muni. They learnt the detailed knowledge of the Vedas in sixty-four days and demonstrated how to suitably honour the spiritual master. Their traditional donation to the teacher came in the form of retrieving Sandipani Muni’s son from the abode of Yamaraja, the god of death.

    Kamsa Killed

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Kamsa Killed Chapter 41, 42, 43, 44 Entering Mathura: As Krishna and Balarama entered the opulent city of Mathura, the residents were mesmerised. Their minds were captivated and their hearts melted; everyone stopped to drink the beauty of the brothers through their eyes. The exception was a miserly washerman, who, when he rudely refused to gift Krishna some garments, lost his head! A pious weaver, who generously gifted Them ornaments, was benedicted, while the florist, Sudama, welcomed the transcendental brothers into his home with a warm reception. Breaking the Bow: After offering her finest oils to Krishna, Trivakra’s hunchbacked body was miraculously straightened by Krishna. The Supreme Lord then proceeded to the wrestling arena. There, Krishna broke the sacrificial bow and annihilated the guards who tried to attack Him. Hearing of these events, Kamsa was beset with anxiety since every sign he saw spelt doom. The following morning, crowds filled the arena, and Kamsa became more and more apprehensive. Killing Kuvalayapida: When Krishna arrived at the arena gate, He was greeted with an attack from Kuvalayapida, the mighty elephant. After a playful tussle, Krishna extracted the elephant’s tusk and used it to beat him and his keepers to death. When Krishna entered the arena, the various personalities there perceived Him in different ways according to their character and consciousness. They all chattered amongst themselves, recounting the extraordinary activities of Krishna in Vrindavana. Just then, Chanura appeared and insisted on a personal duel with Krishna. Killing Kamsa: The two professional wrestlers, Chanura and Mustika, enthusiastically jumped in for a fight, though Krishna and Balarama expertly manoeuvered themselves to remain unharmed. The onlookers complained that it was an unfair duel since Kamsa’s agents were much older. Krishna soon mitigated their anxiety by tossing Chanura onto the ground and ending his life, while Balarama followed suit with Mustika. When the other wrestlers attempted to intervene, they also lost their lives. Kamsa was aghast! When the evil King ordered his henchmen to kill Vasudeva, Krishna furiously leapt onto the royal dais where he sat. He threw Kamsa onto the floor of the wrestling ring and brought his life to an end. When the evil King’s widowed wives lamented, Krishna consoled them and arranged for the funeral rites.

    Uddhava in Vrindavana / Akrura in Hastinapura

    Canto 10 (Part 2)

    M – Mathura-Lila (41-51) Uddhava in Vrindavana / Akrura in Hastinapura Chapter 46, 47, 48, 49 Thinking about His beloved devotees in Vrindavana, Krishna asked His intimate friend, Uddhava, to deliver a message to them. He also wanted Uddhava, an advanced spiritualist himself, to witness the unique emotions of love in separation that they embodied - the love of Vrindavana’s residents is unparalleled. Upon arrival, Uddhava was enchanted by the beauty and spirituality of Vrindavana, and was particularly inspired by Nanda and Yasoda, whose absorption in Krishna was profound. He reassured them that the Lord would return soon. Uddhava then approached the gopis , who were astounded by how much he resembled Krishna. In the pain of separation from their beloved Krishna, the gopis questioned the motives of His friendship with them. When one gopi saw a bee and considered it a messenger of Krishna, she poetically expressed her feelings of transcendental anger in separation. To comfort them, Uddhava read Lord Krishna’s message, wherein He told the gopis “I am the Supreme Soul and Supreme shelter of all, but to increase your attraction and intensify your remembrance of Me I left you.” With heartfelt emotion, they expressed their hopes, confusions, pains and incredible appreciation for Krishna. Uddhava stayed there for several months longer to witness the exalted nature of their love and share more narrations about Krishna. He eventually returned to Mathura and described all that he had witnessed. Uddhava prayed to take birth as a creeper in Vrindavana, just so he would be blessed with the footdust of those exalted associates of Krishna. After hearing Uddhava’s report, Krishna, as promised, visited Trivakra and satisfied her lusty desires. Krishna then visited Akrura, who welcomed Him graciously. The Lord requested him to visit Hastinapura to ascertain how the Pandavas, now without their father, were coping with the difficult situation. In Hastinapura, Vidura and Kuntidevi relayed how Dhritarastra’s envious sons were conspiring to destroy the saintly Pandavas. Kunti sincerely prayed that Krishna comes to the rescue. Akrura delivered Krishna’s advice to Dhritarastra, reminding him of the temporary nature of family relationships and the dangers of bodily consciousness, but the blind King expressed his inability to follow. These words of wisdom, he said, were simply like lightning flashes – though illuminating, the darkness of ignorance kept returning. After staying there for several months and analysing the situation, Akrura left for Mathura.

    Important Words
    • śyāmam — dark blue
      The Gauḍīya signature complexion of Bhagavān — ghana-śyāma, the rain-cloud hue that the gopīs, Yaśodā and the cowherd boys drink with their eyes. Not a generic 'blue god'; this exact śyāma is what Nārada had described to Kālayavana as the mark of Vāsudeva.
    • śrīvatsa-lāñchanaḥ — marked with Śrīvatsa
      Compound: śrīvatsa (the curl of hair on the Lord's chest, the resting-place of Lakṣmī) + lāñchanaḥ (bearing as a mark). One of the diagnostic Vaiṣṇava lakṣaṇas — Bhagavān alone bears it; demigods do not.
    • catuḥ-bhujaḥ — four-armed
      Bhagavān's aiśvarya-form here briefly displaces the two-armed Vraja-Kṛṣṇa, so that the lakṣaṇas Nārada specified can be confirmed. Gauḍīyas note that Kṛṣṇa shows whichever form serves the līlā — four arms to convince Kālayavana, two arms for Vraja's intimacy.
    • vāsudevaḥ — Vāsudeva, son of Vasudeva
      The name under which Bhagavān is worshiped as the omnipresent Supreme — vasati sarvatra iti vāsudevaḥ. Kālayavana names Him correctly even while attacking; even asuric recognition is a kind of remembrance, and Mucukunda will redeem this same name in stuti.
    • nārada-proktaiḥ — described by Nārada Muni
      Compound: nārada + proktaiḥ (declared). The Vaiṣṇava lakṣaṇas reach even Kālayavana through Nāradīya transmission. Paramparā is so potent that an asura can identify Bhagavān correctly when a pure devotee has told him what to look for.
    • durāpam — difficult to attain
      From dur (difficult) + āp (attain). The very Lord whom yogīs cannot catch in meditation deliberately makes Himself appear catchable to Kālayavana — His durāpatva and His sulabhatva (easy approachability) are the same compassion seen from two angles.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Kālayavana saw the Lord come out from Mathurā like the rising moon. The Lord was most beautiful to behold, with His dark-blue complexion and yellow silk garment. Upon His chest He bore the mark of Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha gem adorned His neck. His four arms were sturdy and long. He displayed His ever-joyful lotuslike face, with eyes pink like lotuses, beautifully effulgent cheeks, a pristine smile and glittering shark-shaped earrings. The barbarian thought, “This person must indeed be Vāsudeva, since He possesses the characteristics Nārada mentioned: He is marked with Śrīvatsa, He has four arms, His eyes are like lotuses, He wears a garland of forest flowers, and He is extremely handsome. He cannot be anyone else. Since He goes on foot and unarmed, I will fight Him without weapons.” Resolving thus, he ran after the Lord, who turned His back and ran away. Kālayavana hoped to catch Lord Kṛṣṇa, though great mystic yogīs cannot attain Him.
    Purport

    Although Kālayavana was seeing Lord Kṛṣṇa with his own eyes, he could not adequately appreciate the beautiful Lord. Thus instead of worshiping Kṛṣṇa, he attacked Him. Similarly, it is not uncommon for modern men to attack Kṛṣṇa in the name of philosophy, “law and order” and even religion.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Kālayavana saw the Lord come out from Mathurā like the rising moon. The Lord was most beautiful to behold, with His dark-blue complexion and yellow silk garment. Upon His chest He bore the mark of Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha gem adorned His neck. His four arms were sturdy and long. He displayed His ever-joyful lotuslike face, with eyes pink like lotuses, beautifully effulgent cheeks, a pristine smile and glittering shark-shaped earrings. The barbarian thought, "This person must indeed be Vāsudeva, since He possesses the characteristics Nārada mentioned: He is marked with Śrīvatsa, He has four arms, His eyes are like lotuses, He wears a garland of forest flowers, and He is extremely handsome. He cannot be anyone else. Since He goes on foot and unarmed, I will fight Him without weapons." Resolving thus, he ran after the Lord, who turned His back and ran away. Kālayavana hoped to catch Lord Kṛṣṇa, though great mystic yogīs cannot attain Him.
    Commentary

    In the fifty first chapter Mucukunda burns up Kalayavana with his glance and satisfies Krsna with his prayers. Krsna gives Mucunda benediction. Though others who are qualified by devotion can appreciate the beauty of Krsna, the asuras cannot taste that beauty even if the Lord is before their eyes, because of their inimical attitude. To show that fact, this verse describes the beauty of Krsna as he stood before Kalayavana. Kalayavana chased Krsna who was fleeing away (pradravantam).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kālayavana saw him coming out of the city. The word vi--niṣkrantam indicates he was certain that Kṛṣṇa had come out. Śukadeva describes Kṛṣṇa, by seeing his real nature out of prema. This is not how Kālayavana saw him, since if he did, he could not have had enmity with him. Nāhaṁ prakāśaḥ sarvasya yoga-māyā-samāvṛtaḥ: being covered by my yoga-māyā, I am not visible at all to the fools. (BG 7.26) Just as a person fond of bitter foods does not appreciate sweet foods, demons see only a dull shadow of the real Kṛṣṇa. Though they see Kṛṣṇa, they do not really see him. Because Kṛṣṇa appeared according to Nārada’s description, with four long, thick arms, because of the distinguishing characteristics related by Nārada, Kālayavana quickly understood that this was Kṛṣṇa. He had eyes pink like a fresh lotus. According to Amara-koṣa, aruṇa means very pale red. His cheeks possessed beauty (śrīmat). The suffix mat is used to suggest praise. Sukapola indicates the excellence of his body parts. He smiled because of pleasure. His earrings and other ornaments as well sparkled (sphūran). The first three verses describe Kṛṣṇa. Kālayavana thought, “This must be Vāsudeva. It cannot be anyone else.” He then describes Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa was going at quite a fast pace in a playful manner (pra—ā—dravantam). Out of pride Kālayavana wanted to catch him. But because Kṛṣṇa was difficult to catch even for yogīs, Kālayavana would be a laughing stock.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kālayavana saw him coming out of the city, strolling at a casual pace, alone (vi-niṣkrantam). He was like the rising moon, a disc of light which gives joy to the mind and eye. Thus he saw the Lord clearly (vilokya), though he was at a distance. He is depicted as most beautiful. Nārada, having always seen the four armed form, described this to Kālayavana. Thus he saw Kṛṣṇa in his form now. His eyes were red like fresh lotuses. Also implied by the word nava (new) are the eyes’ wideness and happiness since these are constant qualities of his eyes. He was ever joyful and thus endowed with all beauty (śrīmat). Another cause of beauty is mentioned. He was endowed with or manifested (vibhrāṇam) beautiful cheeks, smile and lotus face. This person must be the son of Vasudeva, with extraordinary qualities like the Śrīvatsa mark. He was most beautiful with the lotus garland extending to his feet. The previously mentioned details of his form are also understood in what Kālayavana described. He recognized the Lord by what Nārada had described (iti). Or he thought (iti), “It cannot be anyone else.” He then decided, “Since he has no weapons I will also fight without weapons.” Kṛṣṇa was walking slightly fast, and casually (prādravantam). He wanted to catch Kṛṣṇa, out of pride, and because he thought he could do it. He pursued Kṛṣṇa on foot, though Kṛṣṇa could not be caught by yogīs. This shows the demon’s foolishness.

    Personal Guidance
    Kālayavana sees the Lord emerge from Mathurā like the rising moon — dark-blue, yellow-silk, Śrīvatsa-marked, Kaustubha-glowing, four-armed in essence, beautifully ornamented. Even seeing Him directly, the wicked cannot adequately appreciate; sight is not yet vision.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you see something true but fail to worship it because you can't yet perceive its weight?
    • What grace would shift your seeing into actual recognition?
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa walking unarmed out of Mathurā is the moon rising over a dark fortress — beauty itself stepping into the open, drawing the enemy outward. Kālayavana sees the four arms, Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, makara earrings — every detail Nārada had described — and concludes, 'This must be Vāsudeva.' Even a barbarian, given the Vaiṣṇava lakṣaṇas in advance, can recognize Bhagavān when He appears.

    Stories
    Akrūra at the river

    Earlier in this same canto (SB 10.39), Akrūra, on his way to Mathurā, sees Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma in the Yamunā exactly as the śāstras describe — śyāma, four-armed in vision, marked with Śrīvatsa, garlanded with vanamālā. He recognizes Bhagavān by the lakṣaṇas because Nārada and the Bhāgavata tradition had given him the map.

    Kālayavana's recognition here is the asuric mirror of Akrūra's: same lakṣaṇas, same Vāsudeva, but pursued with weapons rather than with prayers. The form is identical; the mood determines the fruit.

    Important Words
    • hariṇā — by Lord Kṛṣṇa
      Instrumental of Hari — He who steals (harati) the hearts of His devotees and the sins of the surrendered. Even when fleeing, Kṛṣṇa is the active agent; Kālayavana imagines he is the hunter, but Hari is the one leading.
    • pade pade — at each step
      Reduplication for emphasis — at every single footfall. Bhagavān's līlā is not coarse-grained; He calibrates each step so that the asura's hope is renewed and then frustrated, drawing him exactly to Mucukunda's cave.
    • darśayatā — by Him who was showing
      Present participle of √dṛś, causative. Kṛṣṇa is darśayitā — the One who shows. He shows Himself as catchable so He can show Mucukunda as the burner. Every darśana He grants is itself a teaching.
    • yavana-īśaḥ — the king of the Yavanas
      Compound: yavana (barbarian, foreigner) + īśaḥ (lord). Kālayavana is 'lord' of the mlecchas but is being led like a beast by the actual Īśvara. The repeated īśa-vocabulary in this chapter is deliberate — Mucukunda will later use īśa for Kṛṣṇa, contrasting true lordship with pretended lordship.
    • kandaram — cave
      The cave is Bhagavān's chosen instrument. Gauḍīyas read this as a paradigm: Kṛṣṇa pre-arranges the geography of His līlā so that the devotee Mucukunda — sleeping for ages — is exactly where He needs him at the precise moment. Nothing in His pastimes is accidental.
    Appearing virtually within reach of Kālayavana’s hands at every moment, Lord Hari led the King of the Yavanas far away to a mountain cave.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Appearing virtually within reach of Kālayavana's hands at every moment, Lord Hari led the King of the Yavanas far away to a mountain cave.
    Commentary

    Krsna led Kalayavana far off to a cave in the mountain, by letting himself almost get caught, and then running away time and time again.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This verse shows the dexterity of the Lord. Kālayavana was led by Kṛṣṇa whom he saw at every moment, almost in his hands, far away to a mountain cave.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though he was king of the Yavanas, he was led away by Kṛṣṇa, who encouraged him by showing himself to be at arm’s length.

    Personal Guidance
    Appearing virtually within reach at every moment, Hari leads the King of the Yavanas far away to a mountain cave. The Lord can lead an enemy precisely where He intends; apparent pursuit is actually being led.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you imagine yourself pursuing when you are actually being led?
    • How could the cave you're heading toward be the Lord's plan?
    Analogy

    A cowherd leading a strong but blind bull by holding a stick just past its horns — always within reach, never reached. Kṛṣṇa lets His hand seem to brush Kālayavana's grasp at every step, drawing the doomed king exactly to the cave-mouth He has chosen. The 'flight' of Bhagavān is a route, not a retreat.

    Important Words
    • palāyanam — fleeing
      From parā-√i. Kālayavana names what he sees, but he misreads it. Bhagavān's palāyana is never fear; it is līlā-strategy. The Yadu-lineage 'rule' he cites is a kṣatriya-dharma fragment used by an asura who has no dharma.
    • yadu-kule — in the Yadu dynasty
      Compound: yadu (descendant of Yayāti's son Yadu) + kule (in the dynasty). Bhagavān's chosen lineage in this avatāra — the dynasty Vasudeva, Devakī, Nanda, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa adorn. Even an asura must invoke it, because everyone in the universe knows where Bhagavān has descended.
    • kṣipan — insulting, hurling
      Present participle of √kṣip (to throw). Kālayavana hurls words because he cannot hurl himself onto Kṛṣṇa. Verbal aparādha against Bhagavān is the precise mark of the un-cleansed heart — and it is the cause, the very next clause states, that he cannot reach Him.
    • ahata-aśubhaḥ — whose sinful reactions are not cleansed
      Compound: a (not) + hata (destroyed) + aśubhaḥ (inauspiciousness, sin). The hidden cause of his failure. Gauḍīyas read this as the diagnostic verse for darśana itself: without pāpa-kṣaya, Kṛṣṇa's nearness is no nearness at all. Mucukunda, by contrast, has the burning glance because his austerities cleansed him.
    • prāpa — he reached
      Aorist of √āp — the same root as durāpam (verse 6). The asura cannot prāpta what the yogī cannot prāpta — only because in his case the inability is punitive, not gracious.
    While chasing the Lord, the Yavana cast insults at Him, saying “You took birth in the Yadu dynasty. It’s not proper for You to run away!” But still Kālayavana could not reach Lord Kṛṣṇa, because his sinful reactions had not been cleansed away.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    While chasing the Lord, the Yavana cast insults at Him, saying "You took birth in the Yadu dynasty. It's not proper for You to run away!" But still Kālayavana could not reach Lord Kṛṣṇa, because his sinful reactions had not been cleansed away.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seeing he could not catch Kṛṣṇa, Kālayavana began scolding him in order to stop him. Since Kṛṣṇa was famous among the Yadus for his courage, he should not flee. Scolding him, he followed him, but could not catch him at all (pra—āpa). The reason is ahata-śubhaḥ, literally “he had not destroyed his sins.” Since his sins were eradicated by suddenly seeing the Lord, presence of sin cannot be the cause of his not attaining the Lord. One could propose that if Kālayavana’s auspiciousness were unimpeded, he would have caught his enemy. However, he could not catch Kṛṣṇa because of his inimical mentality and actions. One should not lament that Kālayavana did not get libration, since he did attain liberation later. However, just with the destruction of their sins, demons do not attain the Lord: ye ca pralamba-khara-dardura-keśy-ariṣṭa- mallebha-kaṁsa-yavanāḥ kapi-pauṇḍrakādyāḥ | anye ca śālva-kuja-balvala-dantavakra- saptokṣa-śambara-vidūratha-rukmi-mukhyāḥ || ye vā mṛdhe samiti-śālina ātta-cāpāḥ kāmboja-matsya-kuru-sṛṣjaya-kaikayādyāḥ | yāsyanty adarśanam alaṁ bala-pārtha-bhīma- vyājāhvayena hariṇā nilayaṁ tadīyam || The demons headed by Pralambha, Dhenuka, Baka, Keśī, Ariṣṭa, the wrestlers, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Kaṁṣa, Kālayavana, Dvivida, Pauṇḍraka, Śālva, Narakāsura, Balvala, Dantavakra, the seven bulls, Śambara, Vidūratha and Rukmi, as well as those with bow in hand glorious in fighting on the battlefield, such as the Kāmbojas, Matsyas, Kurus, Sṛṣjayas, and Kaikayas will attain sāyujya or Vaikuṇṭha by the Lord or through his instruments Balarāma, Arjuna, Bhīma and others. SB 2.7.34 The Lord cannot be attained by any ordinary means: yat-pāda-pāṁsur bahu-janma-kṛcchrato dhṛtātmabhir yogibhir apy alabhyaḥ sa eva yad-dṛg-viṣayaḥ svayaṁ sthitaḥ kiṁ varṇyate diṣṭam ato vrajaukasām Svayam Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa, whose foot dust cannot be seen by yogīs in samādhi who have controlled their mind by severe hardship for many births, is eternally situated here, directly visible to the eyes of the people of Vraja. Ah! How can the good fortune of the people of Vraja be described? SB 10.12.12 The special means is indicated for attaining the Lord: bhaktyāham ekayā grāhyaḥ śraddhayātmā priyaḥ satām bhaktiḥ punāti man-niṣṭhā śva-pākān api sambhavāt Only by bhakti with full faith can the devotees obtain me, Paramātmā, the object of love. Bhakti fixed in me purifies even a dog eater of his low birth. SB 11.14.21 pāda-saṁvāhanaṁ cakruḥ kecit tasya mahātmanaḥ apare hata-pāpmāno vyajanaiḥ samavījayan Some of the cowherd boys, who were all great souls, would then massage his lotus feet, and others, qualified by being free of all sin, would expertly fan the Supreme Lord. SB 10.15.17 In the above verse hata-pāpmānaḥ refers to the highest bhakti devoid completely of indifferent or hostile attitude towards the Lord. Thus in the verse the phrase ahata-aśubhaḥ means his inimical attitude towards the Lord. How could he attain the Lord in the manner that Yaśodā caught him as he ran away?

    Personal Guidance
    Kālayavana insults the Lord while chasing — 'You took birth in the Yadu dynasty; it's not proper for You to run away!' — but cannot reach Him because his sinful reactions are not cleansed. Insult doesn't change distance; karma maintains the gap.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where does your unfinished karma keep you from reaching what you chase?
    • How does honest reckoning narrow the gap insults can't?
    Analogy

    A father who refuses to wrestle a drunken stranger is not weak — he is unwilling to dignify the contest. Kālayavana's taunt ('Yadu-born, you must not flee!') misreads Kṛṣṇa's grace as cowardice. His sins are still un-burned, so the contact he craves is the contact he cannot have.

    Stories
    Jarāsandha's seventeen defeats

    Earlier in this canto (SB 10.50), Kṛṣṇa retreats from Jarāsandha seventeen times, each time letting the demon think he has won. The Yadus, including Balarāma, are also visibly 'fleeing.' Śrīla Prabhupāda explains that Bhagavān's apparent retreat is a strategic kindness — He reduces the asuric burden of the earth one engagement at a time, on His own timetable.

    With Kālayavana the same principle operates at single-combat scale: the 'flight' is itself the weapon, drawing the asura to the precise cave where his accumulated pāpa will combust.

    Important Words
    • kṣiptaḥ — insulted
      Past participle of √kṣip — picking up the previous verse's kṣipan. Bhagavān absorbs verbal abuse silently and uses it as direction-finding for the asura's destruction. Tolerance of aparādha is not passivity; it is the patience of fire waiting for fuel.
    • bhagavān — the Supreme Lord
      The six opulences in fullness: aiśvarya, vīrya, yaśas, śrī, jñāna, vairāgya. The verse insists on 'bhagavān' precisely when He is being chased like a coward — the irony marks His sva-tantra-tā: He is bhagavān whether or not the asura perceives it.
    • giri-kandaram — the mountain cave
      Compound: giri (mountain) + kandaram (cave). The same word-field as verse 7; the geography is now closing on the asura. Mountains and caves in Bhāgavatam often house sleeping devotees and waiting agents of Bhagavān (cf. Jaḍa Bharata, Mārkaṇḍeya).
    • anyam — another
      The 'other person' is the entire pivot of the līlā. The asura sees what he thinks is another sleeping victim; he sees, in fact, his own end. Gauḍīyas note that Kṛṣṇa never strikes Kālayavana Himself — the burning is sourced in a devotee. The Lord protects His name even from the appearance of violence.
    • śayānam — lying down, sleeping
      Present participle of √śī. Mucukunda's sleep is itself a boon-form (verse 21 below) — the demigods gave it, and Kṛṣṇa is now ending it. Sleep in śāstra often masks tapas; Mārkaṇḍeya, Nara-Nārāyaṇa and Mucukunda all reveal great power on waking.
    Although insulted in this way, the Supreme Lord entered the mountain cave. Kālayavana also entered, and there he saw another man lying asleep.
    Purport

    The Lord exhibits here His opulence of renunciation. Determined to execute His plan and give His blessings to Mucukunda, the Lord ignored Kālayavana’s insults and calmly proceeded with His program.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    Kalayavana saw another person.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord, omniscient, knew the power and bhakti of his devotee Mucukunda who was sleeping in the cave. When he entered the cave it is understood that he stood near Mucukunda’s head. śiraḥsthāne tu rājarṣer mucukundasya keśavaḥ / saṁdarśana-pathaṁ tyaktvā tasthau buddhimatāṁ varaḥ // Kṛṣṇa, the best of the intelligent, stood near the head of king Mucukunda without being visible. He did so to make room for Kālayavana and to hide himself. He did not see the Lord, but someone else. Hari-vaṁśa

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.51.10

    ↗
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "So, after leading me such a long distance, now He is lying here like some saint!" Thus thinking the sleeping man to be Lord Kṛṣṇa, the deluded fool kicked him with all his strength.
    Commentary

    By the angry glance from Mucunda, Kalayavana’s body caught on fire, and then that fire generated from Kalayavana’s own body burned him up and turned him to ashes. This was because of the boon prayed for and received by Mucukunda. This is mentioned in the Hari vamsa: "Mucukunda repeatedly said "O devatas, may that person who wakes me from sleep be burned up by my eyes fiery with anger." He prayed for the boon of sleep because of the words of the ancient sage Garga. "I will remain asleep, without waking until Krsna appears. It is impossible for me, longing for the sight of Krsna, to remain awake for many cycles of four yugas. By sleeping, that time will pass in a few moments." He prayed for the boon of burning up the waker’s body by his angry eyes to instill fear in Indra, who may try to wake him up to destroy more of Indra’s enemies. This boon was granted as described in the Visnu Purana: The devas said, "He who wakes up Mucukunda from sleep will instantly turn to ashes by the fire from his body."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kālayavana did not think that Kṛṣṇa could not go anywhere else. He did not consider how Kṛṣṇa could suddenly be lying down. How could he consider this to be Kṛṣṇa, since the form he saw did not have four arms? He was fooled (mūḍhaḥ), because of the deep darkness and his anger.

    Important Words
    • utthāya — having risen
      Absolutive of ut-√sthā. Mucukunda's ut-thāna prefigures the deeper ut-thāna of his consciousness: he rises from physical sleep, and within a few verses will rise from the sleep of material identification into bhakti.
    • ciram — for a long time
      Marks the immensity of his sleep — yuga-spans, granted by the demigods. The Bhāgavata pacing slows here to honor it: a tapasvī who served Indra is now waking exactly when Kṛṣṇa is in the room. Kāla is Kṛṣṇa's instrument; the timing belongs to Him.
    • śanaiḥ — slowly
      Adverb — gently, by degrees. The verse refuses to rush the waking; even narrative tempo reverences the ṛṣi. Gauḍīyas read this slowness as a counterweight to Kālayavana's frantic chase: bhakti-pace versus asura-pace.
    • locane — his two eyes
      Dual of locana. These are the eyes whose glance will next combust the asura. The poet lingers on the opening of the eyes precisely because their darśana is, in the next verse, lethal — and elsewhere in the Bhāgavata redemptive.
    • avasthitam — standing
      Past participle of ava-√sthā. Kālayavana is sthita in the wrong place at the wrong moment, while Kṛṣṇa has just entered and stepped aside. The verb-field of standing/lying frames the whole scene: the sleeper rises, the standing one falls.
    The man awoke after a long sleep and slowly opened his eyes. Looking all about, he saw Kālayavana standing beside him.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The man awoke after a long sleep and slowly opened his eyes. Looking all about, he saw Kālayavana standing beside him.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    While he was ruling in the Treta-yuga of the first cycle of yugas in Vaivasvata Manvantara, he went help the devatās. After that he had been sleeping, till the present twenty-eighth cycle. He opened his eyes slowly because of being dizzy from suddenly being wakened by force.

    Reflection Questions
    • Whose appearance might be the alarm that ends your long spiritual sleep?
    • What in your life recently 'woke you up' that you initially saw as enemy?
    Analogy

    A long-banked fire opens its eyes — the cave-darkness, then a figure standing too close. Mucukunda's slow waking is the universe drawing a breath before a verdict; the asura mistakes the sleeper for the disturber, and signs his own death warrant by being the first thing the sage sees.

    Important Words
    • ruṣṭasya — of the angered one
      Genitive past participle of √ruṣ. The wrath is Mucukunda's, but its trigger is Kṛṣṇa's arrangement. Gauḍīyas read the sage's anger as a śakti channel — the same ruṣ that destroys asuras is converted into vinaya by the very next darśana of Bhagavān (verse 22).
    • dṛṣṭi-pātena — by the casting of the glance
      Compound: dṛṣṭi (sight) + pātena (by the falling, casting). The instrument is sight itself. In Vaiṣṇava aesthetics dṛṣṭi-pāta from Bhagavān or His devotee is unfathomably potent — Mahāprabhu's glance liberates; Mucukunda's glance, while still embedded in karma, combusts.
    • deha-jena — generated within his own body
      Compound: deha (body) + jena (born). The fire arises inside Kālayavana himself — his own un-burned aśubha (verse 8) becomes its own pyre. Gauḍīya commentators stress: Kṛṣṇa kills no one; sin destroys itself once the right glance falls.
    • agninā — by fire
      Instrumental of agni. The fire is not Mucukunda's tejas weaponized; it is the asura's pāpa ignited. The Bhāgavata's metaphysics of karma made vivid: every action accumulates its own combustible residue.
    • bhasma-sāt — reduced to ashes
      Compound: bhasma (ash) + sāt (state-of). The same phrase the chapter reuses at verse 22 to mark the moment when Bhagavān, his work done through the sage, reveals Himself. Kālayavana's ash is the threshold of Mucukunda's stuti.
    The awakened man was angry and cast his glance at Kālayavana, whose body burst into flames. In a single moment, O King Parīkṣit, Kālayavana was burnt to ashes.
    Purport

    The man who incinerated Kālayavana with his glance was named Mucukunda. As he will explain to Lord Kṛṣṇa, he had fought for a long time on behalf of the demigods, finally taking as his benediction the right to sleep undisturbed. The Hari-vaṁśa explains that he secured the further benediction of being able to destroy anyone who disturbed his sleep. Ācārya Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura quotes from the Śrī Hari-vaṁśa as follows: prasuptaṁ bodhayed yo māṁ taṁ daheyam ahaṁ surāḥ cakṣuṣā krodha-dīptena evam āha punaḥ punaḥ “Again and again Mucukunda said, ‘O demigods, with eyes blazing with anger, may I incinerate anyone who awakens me from sleep.’” Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī explains that Mucukunda made this rather morbid request to scare Lord Indra, who, Mucukunda thought, might otherwise wake him repeatedly to request his help in fighting Indra’s cosmic enemies. Indra’s consent to Mucukunda’s request is described in Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa as follows: proktaś ca devaiḥ saṁsuptaṁ yas tvām utthāpayiṣyati deha-jenāgninā sadyaḥ sa tu bhasmī-kariṣyati “The demigods declared, ‘Whoever awakens you from sleep will suddenly be burnt to ashes by a fire generated from his own body.’”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The awakened man was angry and cast his glance at Kālayavana, whose body burst into flames. In a single moment, O King Parīkṣit, Kālayavana was burnt to ashes.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    As soon as Mucucunda glanced, Kālayavana burst into flames, and immediately turned to ashes. O Parīkṣit, you were born in a great dynasty (bhārata)! You should not consider such powers astonishing. The benediction from the devatās that he could burn him up with the anger of his glance is inferred, according to Śukadeva, and thus not mentioned. Some verses after verse 20 have been interpolated. Viṣṇu Purāṇa however says this was part of the benediction: proktaś ca devaiḥ saṁsuptaṁ yas tvām utthāpayiṣyati deha-jenāgninā sadyaḥ sa tu bhasmī-kariṣyati The devatās declared, “Whoever awakens you from sleep will suddenly be burnt to ashes by a fire generated from his own body.” Hari-vaṁśa also agrees with this: prasuptaṁ bodhayed yo māṁ taṁ daheyam ahaṁ surāḥ cakṣuṣā krodha-dīptena evam āha punaḥ punaḥ evam astv iti śakras tam uvāca tridaśaiḥ saha / Again and again Mucukunda said, ‘O devatās, with eyes blazing with anger, may I incinerate anyone who awakens me from sleep.” Indra along with the devatās then agreed. Thus it is understood that he prayed that he would sleep until he saw the Lord. Until then it was better to sleep, without being awakened. The reason for awakening is described. He did not want to be awakened again even by a devotee in order to destroy the demons’ armies.

    Personal Guidance
    The awakened Mucukunda casts an angry glance and Kālayavana's body bursts into flame, reduced to ashes. Spiritual potency stored in long sleep can dispatch enemies on a single glance.
    Reflection Questions
    • What sustained spiritual reserve do you have that, if unleashed at the right moment, could end a problem?
    • Where does waiting actually build power?
    Analogy

    A magnifying glass left in a sunbeam — the glance is the lens, the un-burned pāpa is the tinder, and the asura is consumed in a single instant. Mucukunda does not raise a weapon; his accumulated tapas, refracted through one angry look, finishes what Kṛṣṇa's flight began.

    Stories
    Durvāsā's glance and Ambarīṣa

    Mahārāja Ambarīṣa, the great Vaiṣṇava king of SB 9.4, is targeted by the wrath of Durvāsā Muni — and Durvāsā's tapas-fire turns against him only because the Sudarśana cakra, summoned by Ambarīṣa's bhakti, intercedes. There the tapasvī's wrath is neutralized by Bhagavān; here it is directed by Him.

    The parallel is exact in mechanism (tapas turning to fire) and opposite in target. Gauḍīyas read both as proof that Kṛṣṇa is the unseen valve — He routes tapas-fire where He wills, sparing devotees, consuming asuras.

    Important Words
    • brahman — O brāhmaṇa
      Vocative — Parīkṣit addresses Śukadeva. The king under death-sentence is, again and again, the model śravaṇa-practitioner: he asks, the brāhmaṇa speaks, the seven days of the Bhāgavata unfold. Bhakti is sustained by exactly this circuit.
    • vīryaḥ — powers
      From vīrya — heroic potency. Mucukunda has vīrya enough to incinerate an asura with a glance, but the rest of the chapter will show that his real vīrya is the strength to refuse all boons except service. Two senses of vīrya laid side by side.

      Accusative of guhā. The cave will keep returning — it is geography, refuge, and tomb, but most importantly the temple of Mucukunda-stuti. Bhāgavata caves often house transformations (Jaḍa Bharata's, Mārkaṇḍeya's, Mucukunda's).
    • yavana-ardanaḥ — the destroyer of the Yavana
      Compound: yavana + ardanaḥ (afflicter, killer). Parīkṣit already names Mucukunda by what he did, before knowing who he is. In Bhāgavata pedagogy, action precedes identity in the storytelling — fitting for a tradition whose central category is līlā.
    King Parīkṣit said: Who was that person, O brāhmaṇa? To which family did he belong, and what were his powers? Why did that destroyer of the barbarian lie down to sleep in the cave, and whose son was he?
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    King Parīkṣit said: Who was that person, O brāhmaṇa? To which family did he belong, and what were his powers? Why did that destroyer of the barbarian lie down to sleep in the cave, and whose son was he?
    Commentary

    Whose family did he belong to (kasya)? Where did he get his power from (kim viryah)? Whose son was he (kim tejah)?

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Ko nāma should correctly be kim nāma (which name). Or it can mean “Who is this clearly (nāma)?” Who is this person by lineage and what is his name?

    Parīkṣit asks: who was that person, from what family, what powers, why was he asleep, whose son? Curiosity is appropriate when a single act seems disproportionate; the audience naturally wants the backstory.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you skip the backstory that would explain a person's seemingly disproportionate power?
    • What backstories are yours to learn this week?
    Analogy

    A child watching a thunderbolt strike across a field, then turning to the grandfather: 'Who was that man, what was his lineage, why was he asleep?' Parīkṣit's questions are not idle — they are the Bhāgavata's pedagogy. Every great līlā opens out into a back-story so that the devotee can learn the chain of causes.

    Important Words
    • mucukundaḥ iti khyātaḥ — known as Mucukunda
      Phrase: 'celebrated by the name Mucukunda.' The name unlocks identity; the rest of the chapter will be his speech under that name. Gauḍīyas note that he was famous before this moment for tapas, and after it for stuti — the chapter pivots his fame from kṣatriya to Vaiṣṇava.
    • brahmaṇyaḥ — devoted to the brāhmaṇas
      From brahman + yaḥ — one who reveres the brāhmaṇa class and the brahminical principles. A standing royal virtue in the Bhāgavata: Ambarīṣa, Yudhiṣṭhira, Parīkṣit are all brahmaṇyaḥ. The trait predicts his later humility before Kṛṣṇa, whom he will treat as the supreme brāhmaṇa-bandhu.
    • satya-saṅgaraḥ — true to his battle-vow
      Compound: satya (true) + saṅgaraḥ (vow, engagement, battle). Once he gives his word in war, he keeps it — the kṣatriya-dharma summed in two syllables. The same satya-niṣṭhā will reappear when he refuses every material boon Kṛṣṇa offers.
    • ikṣvāku-kule — in the Ikṣvāku dynasty
      Compound: ikṣvāku (the solar-line founder) + kule (in the dynasty). The same dynasty as Rāma. Gauḍīyas relish that Mucukunda is therefore a kinsman of Bhagavān's previous avatāra — Rāma's lineage meeting Kṛṣṇa's person, generations apart.
    • māndhātṛ-tanayaḥ — the son of Māndhātā
      Compound: māndhātṛ (the cakravartī of SB 9.6) + tanayaḥ (son). Patronymic placement; the Bhāgavata never lets a devotee float free of paramparā. Even the man who burnt Kālayavana with a glance is, first, somebody's son.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Mucukunda was the name of this great personality, who was born in the Ikṣvāku dynasty as the son of Māndhātā. He was devoted to brahminical culture and always true to his vow in battle.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He was a great devotee (mahān).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The son of Yuvanāśva was Māndhātā, nineteen generations after Ikṣvāku. Māndhātā’s son was the best among people (mahān) because of being a devotee of the Lord. purukutsam ambarīṣaṁ mucukundaṁ ca yoginam: these sons were Purukutsa, Ambarīṣa, and Mucukunda, a great devotee. (SB 9.6.38)

    Personal Guidance
    Mucukunda was born in the Ikṣvāku dynasty, son of Māndhātā, devoted to brahminical culture and always true to his vow in battle. The hidden warrior was already exceptional; his pedigree, devotion, and integrity were stable.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you under-honor pedigree, devotion, and integrity in choosing whom to consult?
    • What integrity in you would 'wake up' if called?
    Analogy

    A great oak that came up from the Ikṣvāku-root — the same lineage as Rāma, the same dynasty that Bhāgavatam's ninth canto traces with reverence. Mucukunda is named, lineaged and placed: son of Māndhātā, devoted to brāhmaṇas, true to his battle-vow. Bhāgavata pedagogy never abstracts a devotee from his soil.

    Stories
    The Ikṣvāku line in SB 9

    Canto 9 of Bhāgavatam (chapters 6–13) traces the Ikṣvāku dynasty in detail — Hariścandra, Sagara, Bhagīratha, Khaṭvāṅga, Raghu, Aja, Daśaratha, Rāma. Māndhātā, Mucukunda's father, appears in SB 9.6.30 as the cakravartī who 'conquered the directions and held the earth as one wheel.'

    Gauḍīyas read the Ikṣvāku lineage as the great Vaiṣṇava parallel to the Yadu line — both dedicated to dharma, both producing avatāras and bhaktas. Mucukunda is the surprising bridge: an Ikṣvāku-son who meets Kṛṣṇa, the Yadu-son, in a cave between the ages.

    Important Words
    • yācitaḥ — requested
      Past participle of √yāc — to beg. Even Indra and the demigods had to come as supplicants. The Bhāgavata enjoys reversing demigod-pride: the masters of the upper worlds beg a human kṣatriya. Bhakti orders are not flat — sometimes the human bhakta is higher than the deva.
    • indra-ādyaiḥ — headed by Indra
      Compound: indra + ādyaiḥ (and others). Gauḍīyas read demigod-instrumentality with care: they are real, powerful, but conditioned. Mucukunda protected them; later (verse 20) they confess they cannot give him liberation — only Viṣṇu can.
    • asurebhyaḥ — from the demons
      Ablative of asura — those opposed to sura (light, dharma). The basic Vaiṣṇava polarity. Mucukunda's sevā to the demigods is dharma at the cosmic scale; the chapter will lift him from that dharma into the higher śaraṇāgati to Bhagavān.
    • paritrastaiḥ — by the terrified
      Past participle of pari-√tras — to tremble all around. The demigods' fear shows that their position is not absolute. The Bhāgavata's hierarchy is consistent: even devas tremble; only Bhagavān is abhaya.
    • ciram — for a long time
      Same word as verse 11. Both his service and his sleep are 'cira' — long. Mucukunda's life is unusually elongated because Bhagavān is keeping him in reserve for this exact darśana. Time is Kṛṣṇa's instrument throughout.
    Begged by Indra and the other demigods to help protect them when they were terrorized by the demons, Mucukunda defended them for a long time.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Begged by Indra and the other demigods to help protect them when they were terrorized by the demons, Mucukunda defended them for a long time.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He was requested by Indra to protect them. He protected them for four yugas (ciram).

    Important Words
    • guham — Kārttikeya (Guha)
      Skanda's name 'Guha' literally means 'cave-born' or 'secret one.' A poetic resonance with the cave (guhā) in which Mucukunda will soon sleep — the demigods' new general is 'cave-named' just as their old servant retires to a cave.
    • svaḥ-pālam — as the protector of heaven
      Compound: svaḥ (heaven, svarga) + pālam (protector). The exact office Mucukunda has been holding. The demigods name the role precisely as they release him — sevā-dharma always names what was done.
    • viramatām — please desist
      Imperative of vi-√ram — to cease, retire. A respectful release. The Bhāgavata never depicts demigods commanding a devotee crudely; they speak as supplicants who have now found their solution.
    • kṛcchrāt — from the troublesome
      Ablative of kṛcchra — distress, difficulty. The demigods acknowledge his sevā cost him hardship. Even in heavenly service there is kṛcchra; only direct service to Bhagavān is, in the Gauḍīya reading, ultimately ānanda-bearing.
    • rājan — O King
      Vocative — even the lokapālas address him with his royal title at the moment of release. The honor is intact; only the burden is lifted.

    Reflection Questions
    • What troublesome guardianship in your life has a successor ready but you haven't let go?
    • How do you recognize when 'Kārttikeya has arrived'?
    Analogy

    A long-serving guard told gently, 'The new captain has arrived — you may rest.' Kārttikeya, Śiva's son, takes over as senā-pati of the demigods, and Mucukunda is honorably discharged. The Bhāgavata stages succession as kindness, not as displacement.

    Stories
    Kārttikeya's birth and command

    Kārttikeya (Guha, Skanda) is born from Śiva's tejas to slay Tāraka, the asura who had terrified the demigods (a story given in detail in Mahābhārata Vana-parva and Skanda Purāṇa, and referenced across the Bhāgavatam). When he reaches the age of generalship, the devas obtain a permanent commander and no longer need a borrowed human kṣatriya.

    Gauḍīyas read this as a typical Vaiṣṇava courtesy: Mucukunda's service is not dismissed, it is completed. The demigods then honor him with boons. Sevā in this tradition always ends in honor, never in being discarded.

    Important Words
    • nara-lokam — the world of men
      Compound: nara (man) + lokam (world). The human plane he gave up. Vaiṣṇava texts distinguish nara-loka (limited, mortal) from Vaikuṇṭha (unlimited, eternal). The demigods are offering him return to the first; only Kṛṣṇa, in this chapter, can offer the second.
    • rājyam — kingdom
      From √rāj — to rule. The very thing he will later (verse 54) thank Kṛṣṇa for having stripped from him by 'spontaneous detachment.' The Bhāgavata sets up the contrast carefully: rājya served as duty is one thing; rājya clung to as identity is bondage.
    • nihata-kaṇṭakam — whose thorns are removed
      Compound: nihata (struck down) + kaṇṭakam (thorn, enemy). His earthly kingdom was pacified before he left. The demigods stress this so he knows he is owed nothing — he had given up an easy possession to render hard service.
    • vīra — O hero
      Vocative — the demigods name him as the kṣatriya-vīra. The same word will be re-spent in verse 31 when he calls Kṛṣṇa puruṣa-vyāghra — true vīratva, by the chapter's end, belongs to Bhagavān, and the bhakta's vīratva is to recognize Him.
    • kāmaḥ — desires
      Plural — the personal kāmas he set aside for sevā. Gauḍīyas note: setting aside kāma for demigod-service is dharma; but kāma can return, as the next verses warn. Only fixing the mind on Bhagavān (verse 61) finally exhausts it.

    Kāma means objects of the senses. Instead of rājyam sometimes rājyāni is seen.

    Kāma means objects of the senses. O valiant one! You are capable of doing this. They use the word te (your or by you) to show affection.

    Important Words
    • tulya-kālīnāḥ — contemporaries
      Compound: tulya (equal) + kālīnāḥ (of-the-time). Everyone time-stamped with you eventually receives the same forwarding-address — non-existence. The Bhāgavata's vocabulary for kāla is precise; this word names exactly the relationship Mucukunda is about to lose.
    • kālitāḥ — carried off by time
      Verbal — they were 'time-d.' Kāla is treated as an active agent. In SB 11.5, Kṛṣṇa says kāla is His own form. Mucukunda's family was not merely lost; they were moved by Bhagavān Himself, in His Time-form.
    • sutāḥ — children
      Plural of suta. The Bhāgavata names what was loved before naming what was lost; pathos is built up specifically. Vaiṣṇavas remember each suta is a separate jīva on a separate trajectory — bound to us in one birth, unbound in the next.
    • mahiṣyaḥ — queens
      From mahiṣī — chief queen. Kingdom-relationships, the most exalted earthly bonds, treated as among the items kāla erases. Gauḍīyas read this verse as the structural counterpart to Yaśodā's eternal bond with Kṛṣṇa: vātsalya in Vraja never decays; mundane vātsalya does.
    • amātya-mantriṇaḥ — ministers and advisers
      Compound: amātya + mantriṇaḥ — the cabinet. Even political loyalty is consumed by kāla. The demigods are dismantling Mucukunda's entire memory of belonging, in preparation for him to belong to Bhagavān alone.
    “The children, queens, relatives, ministers, advisers and subjects who were your contemporaries are no longer alive. They have all been swept away by time.

    "The children, queens, relatives, ministers, advisers and subjects who were your contemporaries are no longer alive. They have all been swept away by time.
    Commentary

    They have been made to move (kalitah).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Amātya refers to followers and mantrinaḥ to more intimate followers. Instead of tulya-kālinaḥ sometimes tulya-kālīyā is seen.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Amātya refers a tax collector and mantrinaḥ to person who give advice. They do not exist now because they have attained other bodies (kālitāḥ) or they have been taken away.

    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Your children, queens, relatives, ministers, advisers, and contemporaries are no longer alive; they've all been swept away by time. The cost of a long service can include outliving everyone you knew.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you under-estimate the loneliness that long service produces?
    • How do you honor someone who has outlived their generation?
    Analogy

    A man returning to his village after a long campaign and finding every familiar face gone — children, wives, ministers, neighbors, all carried away by the current. Kāla has done the work no enemy could. The demigods are not consoling Mucukunda; they are introducing him to the only opponent he cannot defeat.

    Stories
    Yudhiṣṭhira at the gates

    At the end of Mahābhārata's Mausala-parva, Yudhiṣṭhira learns that Kṛṣṇa has departed, the Yādavas have annihilated each other, and Dvārakā has been swallowed by the sea. His brothers begin the great journey north, and one by one fall along the path. Like Mucukunda waking to a world emptied by time, Yudhiṣṭhira walks through a kingdom where everyone he loved has been 'swept away.'

    Gauḍīyas read both episodes as the same teaching: kāla erases everything earthly, and what remains is only what was offered to Bhagavān. Yudhiṣṭhira's final companion is dharma in canine form; Mucukunda's is Kṛṣṇa Himself.

    Important Words
    • kālaḥ — time
      Bhagavān's executive form. In Gītā 11.32 Kṛṣṇa says 'kālo'smi' — I am Time, the destroyer of worlds. Here too, the demigods identify Time with Bhagavān Himself, refusing the Indian-philosophy temptation to make Time an impersonal abstraction.
    • balīyān-balinām — stronger than the strong
      Comparative chain. Balavān is many; balīyān is the one above them all. Vedic Sanskrit's chained comparatives are routinely used in the Bhāgavata to assert Bhagavān's supremacy without abstraction — He is the next-step above whatever you can imagine.
    • bhagavān īśvaraḥ — the Supreme Lord, the controller
      The chapter's two charged Vaiṣṇava titles paired explicitly. Bhagavān names the Personality; īśvara names His controllership. The demigods are confessing, mid-counsel, that the One controlling time is the Person, not a principle.
    • paśu-pālaḥ — a herdsman
      Compound: paśu (cow, animal) + pālaḥ (keeper). The very image Gauḍīyas treasure — Kṛṣṇa as gopa, herding souls. Here the demigods unwittingly anticipate Vraja-līlā: the same Kṛṣṇa who herds Time's cows herds the calves of Vṛndāvana with the same hand.
    • krīḍan — playing
      Present participle of √krīḍ. Bhagavān's relation to creation is līlā, not labor. Even time's grinding is His play. Gauḍīyas insist on this: nothing in Bhagavān's activity is grim necessity; everything, including kāla, is His rasa-game.
    “Inexhaustible time, stronger than the strong, is the Supreme Personality of Godhead Himself. Like a herdsman moving his animals along, He moves mortal creatures as His pastime.
    Purport

    The universe is created to gradually rectify the contaminated souls trying to exploit material nature. The Lord moves the conditioned souls along, according to their karma, through the various stages of spiritual rectification. Thus the Lord is like a herdsman (the word paśu-pāla literally means “protector of animals”), who moves the creatures under his protection to various pastures and watering spots in order to protect them and sustain them. A further analogy is that of a doctor, who moves the patient under his care to various areas of a hospital for diverse kinds of examination and treatment. Similarly, the Lord brings us through the network of material existence in a gradual cleansing process so that we can enjoy our eternal life of bliss and knowledge as His enlightened associates. Thus all of Mucukunda’s relatives, friends and co-workers had long ago been swept away by the force of time, which of course is Kṛṣṇa Himself.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "Inexhaustible time, stronger than the strong, is the Supreme Personality of Godhead Himself. Like a herdsman moving his animals along, He moves mortal creatures as His pastime.
    Commentary

    Who has made them move? This verse answers: time.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Time is called bhagavān since it is non-different from the Lord as his śakti. Thus time is called the controller (īśvaraḥ). It is never exhausted (avyayaḥ). It is a continuous flow without beginning or end. It leads (kālayate) all beings. What is its purpose? It is its play. This shows time’s power. It is like a herdsman herding his animals. This shows time’s independence.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Time is the strongest among the strong because it is the Lord, Nārāyaṇa. The aṁśa is non-different from the aṁśī (the Lord). The Lord is endowed with all powers. He does not decrease since he is infinite. He moves all creatures somewhere else (kālayate), in order to play. It is his play. Or he never tires in this action. His power is shown: he does it like play, as a pastime just as a cowherd gathers cows as play at a certain time. The cowherd is the master of the cows, moving them according to his will.

    Personal Guidance
    Inexhaustible time, stronger than the strong, is the Supreme Lord Himself; like a herdsman, He moves mortal creatures as His pastime. Time is not impersonal — it is a face of the Lord at play with creatures.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you treat time as impersonal and miss its theological face?
    • How does seeing time as Kṛṣṇa's play change your reading of recent losses?
    Analogy

    A herdsman walking behind his cows at evening — they go where he taps the staff, eat where he stops them, settle where he speaks. The demigods name Bhagavān-as-Time the cosmic gopāla, with mortal beings as the herd. The image is not impersonal: Kṛṣṇa is, even as Time, the cowherd boy.

    Important Words
    • varam — a benediction
      From vṛ — to choose. The Bhāgavata's standard reward-vocabulary. Varas are limited to what the giver actually owns; the demigods own karma-rewards within saṁsāra, but not mukti.
    • kaivalyam — liberation
      From kevala — alone, exclusive. Kaivalya in non-Gauḍīya schools sometimes means the soul's isolation from prakṛti, even from Bhagavān. Gauḍīyas accept that only Viṣṇu can give liberation but redefine the destination as eternal sevā at His feet, not isolation.
    • bhagavān-viṣṇuḥ — the Supreme Lord, Viṣṇu
      The demigods name the only One competent. Notice the doctrinal precision: not 'the gods,' not 'the absolute' — bhagavān viṣṇuḥ. Gauḍīyas read this as svayam-bhagavān surfacing through demigod speech; even Indra confesses Viṣṇu's monopoly on mukti.
    • ekaḥ-eva — one alone
      Phrase — 'only one.' Stark monotheistic point inside a polytheistic frame. The Bhāgavata's vocabulary admits many devas but insists on one liberator. Acintya-bhedābheda lives precisely here: many distinct devas, one Bhagavān to whom they all defer.
    • avyayaḥ — the inexhaustible
      From a-vi-√i — not subject to decay. The same epithet used in Gītā 7.25 and 10.3 for Bhagavān. Demigods exhaust; Viṣṇu does not. Mucukunda will hear this and, by verse 55, refuse every boon except service to the avyaya.
    “All good fortune to you! Now please choose a benediction from us — anything but liberation, since only the infallible Supreme Lord, Viṣṇu, can bestow that.”
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "All good fortune to you! Now please choose a benediction from us—anything but liberation, since only the infallible Supreme Lord, Viṣṇu, can bestow that."
    Commentary

    Only Visnu can grant that liberation (tasya).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Good fortune to you! This is their general blessing. “Ask a boon.” This is their particular blessing. Kaivalyam means freedom from saṁsāra and attainment of the spiritual world. Viṣṇu is the only person capable of bestowing it (īśvaraḥ) since he is endowed with all powers (bhagavān), inexhaustible though giving benedictions to unlimited people. He is not like us, who have very little power. We become weak by doing austerities etc.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Good fortune! They say this because they were very pleased with him. Or everything is auspicious for you. Now ask for a boon. Or ask for some auspicious boon, except for liberation or exclusive devotion to the Lord’s feet. Only the Lord endowed with all powers can give this (īśvaraḥ) or is its master. Liberation depends on him. By giving himself he is not depleted (avyayaḥ). Since he is spread inside and outside (viśṇuḥ) he has the power to bestow such a condition of being everywhere: he can award liberation.

    Choose a benediction — anything but liberation, since only Viṣṇu can bestow that. Demigods give what they can; what is beyond them they openly acknowledge.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you ask of demigod-level sources what only the Lord can give?
    • How does demigod honesty about their limits guide your own asks?
    Analogy

    A wealthy patron telling a long-serving employee, 'Choose any gift — but not citizenship in another country; that's not mine to give.' The demigods know their jurisdiction. Liberation is not in their treasury, only in Viṣṇu's. The verse is a precise theology of what devas can and cannot do.

    Important Words
    • abhivandya — saluting
      Absolutive of abhi-√vand — to honor, salute. A devotee never simply walks away from those he served; he honors them first. Vaiṣṇava decorum, on display even before Mucukunda meets Kṛṣṇa.
    • mahā-yaśāḥ — of great fame
      Compound: mahā + yaśāḥ (fame). The Bhāgavata pauses to honor him with an epithet at the moment of his withdrawal from the world. Yaśas in Vaiṣṇava texts is one of the six bhaga-opulences; here it is conferred on the devotee because of his sevā.
    • aśayiṣṭa — he lay down
      Aorist of √śī. The same verb-field as verses 9 and 11. Mucukunda enters the posture in which Kṛṣṇa will, eons later, find him. Bhakti's geography includes places where one waits asleep until Bhagavān arrives.
    • guhā-viṣṭaḥ — entering a cave
      Compound: guhā + viṣṭaḥ (entered). The cave is now claimed as his. The chapter's repeated cave-vocabulary (kandara, guhā) marks it as a Vaiṣṇava tīrtha-in-the-making — wherever Bhagavān appears becomes holy.
    • nidrayā — by sleep
      Instrumental of nidrā. The boon itself was sleep. Gauḍīyas note the irony: the demigods could not give kaivalya, so they gave the deepest mundane peace — sleep. Bhagavān will exceed that gift by giving wakefulness in bhakti (verse 61).
    Addressed thus, King Mucukunda took his respectful leave of the demigods and went to a cave, where he lay down to enjoy the sleep they had granted him.
    Purport

    Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura gives the following lines from an alternate reading of this chapter. These lines are to be inserted between the two halves of this verse: nidrām eva tato vavre sa rājā śrama-karṣitaḥ yaḥ kaścin mama nidrāyā bhaṅgaṁ kuryād surottamāḥ sa hi bhasmī-bhaved āśu tathoktaś ca surais tadā svāpaṁ yātaṁ yo madhye tu bodhayet tvām acetanaḥ sa tvayā dṛṣṭa-mātras tu bhasmī-bhavatu tat-kṣaṇāt “The King, exhausted by his labor, then chose sleep as his benediction. He further stated, ‘O best of the demigods, may whoever disturbs my sleep be immediately burned to ashes.’ The demigods replied, ‘So be it,’ and told him, ‘That insensitive person who wakes you in the middle of your sleep will immediately turn to ashes simply by your seeing him.’”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Addressed thus, King Mucukunda took his respectful leave of the demigods and went to a cave, where he lay down to enjoy the sleep they had granted him.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He is called famous because of the following. What use are the devatās if only Viṣṇu can bestow the spiritual world? I do not want to see others. I should sleep alone near Mathurā, dear to the Lord until I can see the Lord. Therefore I will ask of the benediction of sleep. For this reason his famous was spread everywhere. With permission granted by the devatās he lay in the cave. This cave is well known. It is situated in a mountain of Davalapura, south of Mathurā district. In Varāha Purāṇa, in describing parikrama of Mathurā, it is said to be situated within Mathurā. There is a temple made to resemble the cave there, similar to the cave of Yaśodā.

    Important Words
    • bhasma-sāt — reduced to ashes
      Same compound as verse 12 — ash-state. The chapter signals scene-change by reusing the phrase: the asura is now closed business; the devotee-darśana now opens.
    • sātvata-ṛṣabhaḥ — the greatest hero of the Sātvatas
      Compound: sātvata (the clan of pure devotees, the Yadu-Vṛṣṇi lineage) + ṛṣabhaḥ (bull, greatest). A title prized in the Pāñcarātra tradition. Bhagavān reveals Himself not under His abstract names but under His clan-name — He is the chief of His own devotee-family.
    • ātmānam — Himself
      Reflexive — His own self. Kṛṣṇa does not send a representative, a glow, a voice. He reveals ātman — His Person. Gauḍīyas treasure this verb-construction: darśayām āsa ātmānam — He caused His own Self to be seen.
    • darśayām āsa — He revealed
      Periphrastic perfect of causative √dṛś — He made-seen. Darśana is something Bhagavān grants; it cannot be seized. The whole chapter has been one extended setup for the moment darśana becomes possible.
    • dhī-mate — to the intelligent one
      Compound: dhī (intellect, wisdom) + mate (possessing). Mucukunda is dhī-mān because his mind, despite ages of sleep, immediately recognizes Bhagavān. Gauḍīyas read dhī here as buddhi steered toward Bhagavān — sat-buddhi, not mere intellect.
    After the Yavana was burnt to ashes, the Supreme Lord, chief of the Sātvatas, revealed Himself to the wise Mucukunda.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After the Yavana was burnt to ashes, the Supreme Lord, chief of the Sātvatas, revealed Himself to the wise Mucukunda.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Mucukunda is described as wise because he was fixed in devotion to the Lord.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The supreme Lord who was the best of the Yadus (sātvatarṣabhaḥ) revealed himself. This shows his affection for his devotees. He revealed himself to Mucukunda who was fixed in bhakti (dhīmate). Just as Yavana had seen the Lord as Nārāyaṇa, to Mucukunda he showed a similar form, corresponding to the description given by Garga.

    Personal Guidance
    After the Yavana is burnt to ashes, the Supreme Lord reveals Himself to wise Mucukunda. Hidden divine presence is revealed precisely when the obstacle is removed; Kṛṣṇa was always there waiting.
    Reflection Questions
    • What 'Yavana' might need to burn away in your life before the Lord visibly reveals Himself?
    • Where might He already be present, waiting for an obstacle to clear?
    Analogy

    Once the rough work is done, the King steps into the antechamber and lifts the lamp Himself. With Kālayavana ash, Kṛṣṇa shows Himself to Mucukunda in His own form — dark blue, four-armed, smiling. The whole pursuit was scaffolding for this darśana.
