    Important Words
    • ghana-śyāmam — dark blue like a cloud
      Compound: ghana (rain-cloud) + śyāmam (dark blue). The signature Gauḍīya complexion. The same hue that Vraja-gopīs drink in mādhurya, Mucukunda now drinks in the rasa appropriate to his sambandha — śānta-deepening-into-dāsya.
    • vaijayantyā — with the Vaijayantī garland
      Bhagavān's five-flower garland, hanging to His knees. Marker of His Yadu-form. Gauḍīyas distinguish the vaijayantī (worn by Bhagavān) from the vana-mālā (Vraja's wild-flower garland) — both appear in Bhāgavata, the first more associated with majestic darśana, the second with Vraja-intimacy.
    • anurāga-smita-īkṣaṇam — with affectionately smiling glance
      Compound: anurāga (deep affection) + smita (smile) + īkṣaṇam (glance). This is not aiśvarya-darśana alone; the anurāga is already there, even at first meeting. Bhagavān's reception of any devotee — even one waking from yuga-sleep — is loving.
    • udāra-vikramam — with noble gait
      Compound: udāra (noble, generous) + vikramam (stride, valour). The bhāgavata-poet refuses to draw Bhagavān as static; even His standing is in noble motion. The same vikrama that just outran Kālayavana is now still and gracious before Mucukunda.
    • durdharṣam — unassailable
      From dur (difficult) + √dhṛṣ — He whom none can assail. The exact opposite of Kālayavana's misperception ('one who flees'). The verse insists: this is the Lord whom no demon and no boon can sway.
    • mahā-buddhiḥ — of great intelligence
      Compound: mahā + buddhiḥ. Mucukunda is again named for his discernment — the same dhī-mate of verse 22. Gauḍīyas note: buddhi turned toward Bhagavān is the buddhi-yoga of Gītā 2.41 — vyavasāya-buddhi, fixed, single-pointed.
    As he gazed at the Lord, King Mucukunda saw that He was dark blue like a cloud, had four arms, and wore a yellow silk garment. On His chest He bore the Śrīvatsa mark and on His neck the brilliantly glowing Kaustubha gem. Adorned with a Vaijayantī garland, the Lord displayed His handsome, peaceful face, which attracts the eyes of all mankind with its shark-shaped earrings and affectionately smiling glance. The beauty of His youthful form was unexcelled, and He moved with the nobility of an angry lion. The highly intelligent King was overwhelmed by the Lord’s effulgence, which showed Him to be invincible. Expressing his uncertainty, Mucukunda hesitantly questioned Lord Kṛṣṇa as follows.
    Purport

    It is significant that text 24 states, catur-bhujaṁ rocamānam: “The Lord was seen in the beauty of His four-armed form.” Throughout this great work, we find Lord Kṛṣṇa manifesting His various transcendental forms, most prominently the two-armed form of Kṛṣṇa and the four-armed form of Nārāyaṇa or Viṣṇu. Thus there is no doubt that Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu are nondifferent, or that Kṛṣṇa is the original form of the Lord. These things are sometimes misunderstood, but the great ācāryas, experts in spiritual science, have clarified the matter for us. God in His original form is not merely the creator, maintainer and destroyer, or the punisher of conditioned souls, but rather the infinitely beautiful Godhead, enjoying in His own right, in His own abode. This is the form of Kṛṣṇa, the same Kṛṣṇa who expands Himself into Viṣṇu forms for the maintenance of our bumbling world. Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī mentions that the word śaṅkitaḥ, “having some doubt,” indicates that Mucukunda was thinking, “Is this indeed the Supreme Lord?” He expresses himself frankly in the following verses.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As he gazed at the Lord, King Mucukunda saw that He was dark blue like a cloud, had four arms, and wore a yellow silk garment. On His chest He bore the Śrīvatsa mark and on His neck the brilliantly glowing Kaustubha gem. Adorned with a Vaijayantī garland, the Lord displayed His handsome, peaceful face, which attracts the eyes of all mankind with its shark-shaped earrings and affectionately smiling glance. The beauty of His youthful form was unexcelled, and He moved with the nobility of an angry lion. The highly intelligent King was overwhelmed by the Lord's effulgence, which showed Him to be invincible. Expressing his uncertainty, Mucukunda hesitantly questioned Lord Kṛṣṇa as follows.
    Commentary

    Mucukunda had a doubt (sankitah), "Is this the Supreme Lord?" The lord was unconquerable (durdharsam). Iva in this case is only an ornament.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    With his mind attracted to the great beauty of Kṛṣṇa, Śukadeva again describes him, in order to praise the good fortune of Mucukunda. His chest especially shone (virājitam) with the brilliant Kaustubha gem. This shows that it was superior to other ornaments. In the previous description Kṛṣṇa wore a lotus garland extending to his feet. (vanamālā). Now he was shining with a vaijayantī garland, made of flowers of five colors, according to the descriptions of Garga. Like the Lord himself, all his ornaments had infinite forms. He had new youth (vayasam) which was most beautiful. Conquered by Kṛṣṇa’s powers he slowly began to inquire because he was most intelligent.” Others cannot fool me by wearing the Lord’s dress. Others lack the power to overwhelm me.” This is how he thought. He first thought in various ways (śaṅkitaḥ) in order to dispel his doubts. He began to inquire slowly because it was hard to question the Lord (durdharṣam). Iva is ornamental. Because he was highly intelligent he asked thoroughly (paryapṛcchan). By this it is understood he had great devotion like Prahlāda.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord’s beauty is again described in three verses. That form was shown in a special way at all times (viṛajitam). It shone like a million suns (rocamānam). Or it produced taste for the eyes and mind. He wore a garland of five differently colored flowers. Or he shone with the garland. The lotus garland described by Garga manifested as the vaijayantī garland. His face was happy with a smile and attractive (cāru) from chin to forehead to be seen by all in the three worlds. Other unmentioned elements of beauty should also be understood. His glance was endowed with a smile because of love or with a smile indicating his continual mercy. Or he had eyes along with happiness expressed by the smile of his two red lips. His age of new youth was most beautiful. He had the prowess of a mad elephant. He had beauty in his most powerful arms, waist, and chest. Though Mucukunda was intelligent, he was overpowered by the Lord’s power and became afraid. Eventually he questioned the Lord with choked, confused voice. He was a powerful devotee. Why did he react in this way? The Lord could not be conquered by his prowess (durdharṣam). Or he was effulgent with the brilliance of a million suns. The word iva has no special meaning. Or because of his power, he could not be questioned (durdharṣam). Mucukunda questioned the Lord because his intelligence was deep (mahābuddhiḥ). With questioning, he could not understand the truth. Thus his bhakti would not arise and all his births and actions would be useless. Most of all he thought that he could relish the words of the Lord.

    Personal Guidance
    Mucukunda sees the dark-blue, four-armed Lord in yellow silk, Śrīvatsa on chest, Kaustubha gem, Vaijayantī garland — magnificent in all detail. Devotional vision is precise; it sees the Lord's specific features.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which features of Kṛṣṇa do you most reliably see in your meditation?
    • Where could devotional vision become more detailed in your practice?
    Analogy

    A traveler stepping out of a long night and finding the rising sun has a face. Mucukunda sees what Akrūra saw, what Nārada described, what Kālayavana misread — the dark-blue, four-armed, garlanded, smiling Person. The lakṣaṇas are constant; only the seers differ.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma's last darśana

    On the bed of arrows at Kurukṣetra (SB 1.9), Bhīṣma sees Kṛṣṇa standing before him and describes Him in exactly this Pāñcarātra register — śyāma, four-armed in vision, garlanded with vanamālā, the smiling charioteer. Bhīṣma drinks the darśana with his eyes and departs the body fixed on that form.

    The parallel is precise. Two great kṣatriya devotees, at moments of transition — Bhīṣma into death, Mucukunda from sleep into bhakti — receive identical darśana. Gauḍīyas read this consistency as the Bhāgavata's claim that Bhagavān's form is the same form, eternally; it is the meeting that changes the seer.

    Important Words
    • padbhyām-padma-palāśābhyām — with feet (like) lotus petals
      Phrase: padbhyām (two feet) + padma (lotus) + palāśābhyām (with petals). Vaiṣṇava aesthetics' most precious image — Bhagavān's caraṇāravinda. Gauḍīyas teach that meditation on the lotus feet is the entry-rasa of dāsya-bhakti; Mucukunda's first words honor exactly these.
    • vicarasi — You are walking
      Present of vi-√car — to wander, move about. The same root the demigods used for kāla and Kṛṣṇa will reuse in verse 61 ('wander the earth at will'). Bhagavān's vicaraṇa is His freedom — and He gifts the same freedom to His devotee.
    • giri-gahvare — in a mountain cave
      Compound: giri + gahvare (cavern). A new word for cave (different from kandara, guhā) — the Bhāgavata vocabulary keeps reframing the same place, like a poet circling the central image. The cave is now Mucukunda's confessional.
    • uru-kaṇṭake — full of thorns
      Compound: uru (much) + kaṇṭake (thorny). The cave-floor is rough; Bhagavān's lotus feet should not have crossed it. The motif of Bhagavān's feet wounded for the devotee will return — Rūpa Gosvāmī's verses on Kṛṣṇa's feet bleeding in Vraja's pebbled paths echo here.
    Śrī Mucukunda said: Who are You who have come to this mountain cave in the forest, having walked on the thorny ground with feet as soft as lotus petals?
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śrī Mucukunda said: Who are You who have come to this mountain cave in the forest, having walked on the thorny ground with feet as soft as lotus petals?
    Commentary

    You are walking on the ground full of thorns with lotus petal feet.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He asks the question in two verses. You have come through the forest, to a mountain cave hard to enter, after walking on ground profuse with thorns, with soft lotus feet. This indicates the Lord’s affection for his devotee and his power.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Who are you who have come directly here? It is not proper for you. He speaks with great devotion. To express the Lord’s amazing qualities, he first explains that his soft feet are uninjured by the thorns. Or attracted by the Lord’s great beauty and tenderness he speaks with affection about his lotus feet.

    Who are You, who have come to this cave with feet soft as lotus petals on thorny ground? Wonder at the Lord's gentleness in a rough setting is the first response of the awakened devotee.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where has Kṛṣṇa entered the rough ground of your life with lotus-soft feet?
    • How could noticing that gentleness reframe your story?
    Analogy

    A man waking in the dark to find someone walking barefoot toward him across a thorn-strewn floor — and the feet are lotus petals. Mucukunda's first thought is concern for those feet. The verse's tenderness is Vaiṣṇava: the bhakta worries for Bhagavān before himself.

    Important Words
    • tejasvinām-tejaḥ — the potency of the potent
      Phrase: tejasvinām (of the powerful) + tejaḥ (the potency). Mucukunda's first guess is the most accurate — Gītā 7.10 and 10.36: Kṛṣṇa is the tejas of the tejasvī. Even the demigod-list that follows is implicitly subordinated to this opening line.
    • vibhāvasuḥ — the fire-god
      Agni's epithet — 'whose treasure is light.' The first demigod-candidate the kṣatriya names. Mucukunda has spent his life among devas; his vocabulary is Vedic-deva-rich. The chapter will move him from deva-knowledge to bhāgavata-knowledge.
    • sūryaḥ — the sun-god
      His own Ikṣvāku-dynasty's progenitor (sūrya-vaṁśa). Mucukunda's guess names his own forefather — a poignant detail. He cannot yet imagine that the Person before him is the source of even sūrya.
    • somaḥ — the moon-god
      Soma is the deva of the night sky and of Vedic ritual offering. Pairing sūrya and soma covers the major luminaries. The verse runs through the obvious bright candidates before Mucukunda finally lands on Viṣṇu in verse 29.
    • loka-pālaḥ — ruler of a planet
      Compound: loka (planet, world) + pālaḥ (protector). The general office Mucukunda once helped fill — protectors of svarga. Even his guesses are colored by his sevā-history.
    Perhaps You are the potency of all potent beings. Or maybe You are the powerful god of fire, or the sun-god, the moon-god, the King of heaven or the ruling demigod of some other planet.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Perhaps You are the potency of all potent beings. Or maybe You are the powerful god of fire, or the sun-god, the moon-god, the King of heaven or the ruling demigod of some other planet.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Svit indicates conjecture. Perhaps he is the condensed personality of all effulgence. But this cannot be, because light is meager compared to his effulgence. Śrīdhara Svāmī says tejas means a form of power or light. Tejas cannot refer to form. Viśva-prakāśa says tejas means strength, light, source of light, heroism, influence or semen. There is a version with tejo-mūrtiḥ or tejo-mūrtaḥ. This is a portion of the element tejas. Therefore he is vibhūti of the Lord, the god of the element tejas. But the form here is greater than the god of fire which is much smaller. Perhaps this form is the sun god. But the sun does not remove suffering and give bliss. Perhaps this form is the moon god. But it is also not the moon god. Because of its power it must be Indra. But though Indra is king of the devatās he does not reside everywhere. Perhaps this form is one of the deities of the directions? The word vā indicates a side glance (doubt).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Are you power? If so that power must have a form. Are you the lord of fire? Fire is called bhagavān because of possessing all powers as the vibhūti of bhagavān. The same should be understood in the other statements. Perhaps you are someone else—Brahmā or Śiva.

    Perhaps You are the potency of all potent beings — fire god, sun god, moon, Indra, or some other ruling demigod? Mucukunda guesses cosmic identities; even high guesses fall short of Kṛṣṇa.

    Important Words
    • deva-devānām — of the chief gods
      Compound: deva + devānām (of the devas). The God-of-gods construction. Vaiṣṇava texts often telescope titles this way to point to Bhagavān as the deva-deva — the term Arjuna will use in Gītā 11.
    • trayāṇām — of the three
      Genitive plural — Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva. The trimurti is named only to be transcended; Mucukunda places this Person above all three, anticipating the chapter's monotheistic resolution.
    • puruṣa-ṛṣabham — the foremost of persons
      Compound: puruṣa (Person) + ṛṣabham (bull, foremost). The same ṛṣabha-epithet given to Bhagavān in verse 22. Personalist language throughout: not 'highest principle' but 'foremost Person.'
    • guha-dhvāntam — the darkness of the cave
      Compound: guha (cave) + dhvāntam (darkness). Mucukunda makes the inner cave a metaphor: this Person, by being present, dispels the cave-darkness like a lamp. Gauḍīyas read this as Bhagavān's first sevā to the bhakta — bringing light into the heart's guha.
    • pradīpaḥ — a lamp
      From pra-√dīp — to blaze. The first homely image Mucukunda uses for Kṛṣṇa. The Bhāgavata permits and encourages such everyday analogies; bhakti's idiom is intimate before it is exalted.
    I think You are the Supreme Personality among the three chief gods, since You drive away the darkness of this cave as a lamp dispels darkness with its light.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī points out that with His effulgence Lord Kṛṣṇa dispelled not only the darkness of the mountain cave but also the darkness in Mucukunda’s heart. In Sanskrit the heart is sometimes metaphorically referred to as guha, “cavern,” a deep and secret place.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I think You are the Supreme Personality among the three chief gods, since You drive away the darkness of this cave as a lamp dispels darkness with its light.
    Commentary

    You illuminate the darkness of the cave with your lamp like effulgence, and you illuminate my mind covered in ignorance with jewel like knowledge.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In this verse he concludes that the person must be superior to all those previously mentioned. Among the three you are in the category of Viṣṇu, but are the best of those forms (puruṣarṣabham) since you dispel darkness within and without the cave and the suffering within and without my heart (guhā), just as a lamp dispels darkness and suffering by its light. The example is used since light driving away darkness is experience by everyone. The example does not compare the Lord’s effulgence to that of a lamp.

    I think You are the Supreme Personality among the three chief gods, since You drive away the cave's darkness like a lamp. Inner darkness is dispelled too; vision of the Lord clarifies internal night.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where could one lamp-glance from Kṛṣṇa drive away the dark in your inner cave?
    • What 'darkness' would simply lose its grip in His presence?
    Analogy

    A traveler watching a single lamp brighten a whole cave and concluding: this is no torch, this is the sun in here. Mucukunda's grammar moves from candidates to a verdict — among the three principal Persons, this is the Highest.

    Important Words
    • śuśrūṣatām — of those who are eager to hear
      Desiderative present participle of √śru. Śuśrūṣā — the will to listen — is one of bhakti's nine limbs (śravaṇam). Mucukunda's first sādhana posture is exactly the one Parīkṣit holds and the one the Bhāgavata commends throughout.
    • janma — birth
      From √jan. The first of Kṛṣṇa's 'three coordinates' to be asked. In Gītā 4.9 Bhagavān says janma karma ca me divyam — knowing His birth and activities truly liberates. Mucukunda is already, without knowing it, soliciting the BG 4.9 disclosure.
    • karma — activity
      Bhagavān's karma is divya — transcendental. Gauḍīyas insist karma of the Lord is not bound by karmic law; it is līlā. Mucukunda asks for it; in verse 41 Kṛṣṇa will list Kālanemi, Kaṁsa, Pralamba, and Kālayavana.
    • gotram — lineage
      From gotra — clan, descent. Even Bhagavān has a gotra in līlā (the Yadu-Vṛṣṇi-Sātvata line). Gauḍīyas read this not as a limitation but as His chosen way of being known — Bhagavān always belongs somewhere in His pastimes.
    • nara-pum-gava — O foremost among men
      Compound: nara (man) + pum-gava (bull-among, foremost). Mucukunda is still hedging — calling Him 'best among men' rather than 'Lord of all worlds.' His recognition is gradient; full śaraṇāgati arrives by verse 56.
    O best among men, if You like, please truly describe Your birth, activities and lineage to us, who are eager to hear.
    Purport

    When the Supreme Lord descends to this world, He certainly becomes nara-puṅgava, the most eminent member of human society. Of course, the Lord is not actually a human being, and Mucukunda’s questions will lead to a clarification of this point. Thus the term śuśrūṣatām, “to us, who are sincerely eager to hear,” indicates that Mucukunda is inquiring in a noble way for his own and others’ benefit.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O best among men, if You like, please truly describe Your birth, activities and lineage to us, who are eager to hear.
    Commentary

    Please tell us who want to hear. Mucukunda speaks in the plural to indicate his own high position, in order to get an answer from Krsna. If Krsna thought he was a low class person he would be unworthy of an answer.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O best of men! He addresses him in this way since Kṛṣṇa is acting like a human, touching the earth. Please tell me, eager to hear about your pleasing (avyalīkam) birth, activities and name (gotram). The passive is used to indicate respect for his birth, activities and name. Avyalīkam also mean truthfully. The word vā indicates all the items, or alternatives. Though secret, one of these can be revealed. He says “If it pleases you” out of humility.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though he sees the four armed form directly, he also remembers that devas should not touch the earth. Unable to determine that he is Viṣṇu, he calls to him, considering him to be a remarkable human. O best among men! Because you are the best of humans please describe at your discretion (avyalīkam) your birth. Vyalīka means disagreeable. Or describe truthfully. He speaks in the plural to show great respect on seeing him. Vā means everything, or suggests alternatives. What can I do if you do not describe the birth because it is secret? Or tell what you want to do (karma). If you cannot do that, tell your family lineage and name at least. That is, if you want to. This is uttered out of great politeness.

    Please describe Your birth, activities, and lineage; we are eager to hear. The right response to mystery is to ask for the story, not for power.

    Important Words
    • puruṣa-vyāghra — O tiger among men
      Compound: puruṣa + vyāghra (tiger). A standard epithet of a great kṣatriya, here turned toward Bhagavān. Mucukunda upgrades his vocative each verse — nara-pum-gava (30), puruṣa-vyāghra (31), and finally bhagavān, hare, parā-ātman.
    • aikṣvākāḥ — descendants of Ikṣvāku
      From Ikṣvāku — the solar dynasty's founder. Mucukunda names his dynasty with pride and then immediately undercuts it ('fallen kṣatriyas'). Gauḍīya humility: declare your lineage so that Bhagavān can show you what it is worth.
    • kṣatra-bandhavaḥ — fallen kṣatriyas, kṣatriyas only by connection
      Compound: kṣatra + bandhavaḥ (relatives, by-association). A self-deprecating phrase: 'we are kin to kṣatriyas, not true kṣatriyas.' The bhakta's vocabulary in the presence of Bhagavān — always lower than oneself.
    • mucukundaḥ — Mucukunda
      He names himself only after Kṛṣṇa has been honored. Vaiṣṇava decorum: never present oneself first. The bhakta's self-introduction follows the Lord's darśana.
    • prabho — O Lord
      Vocative of prabhu — master. Mucukunda's vocative vocabulary now includes prabhu, marking the shift from 'foremost among men' toward 'my Lord.' The recognition is mid-formation.
    As for ourselves, O tiger among men, we belong to a family of fallen kṣatriyas, descendants of King Ikṣvāku. My name is Mucukunda, my Lord, and I am the son of Yauvanāśva.
    Purport

    It is common in Vedic culture that a kṣatriya will humbly introduce himself as kṣatra-bandhu, a mere relative in a kṣatriya family, or in other words a fallen kṣatriya. In ancient Vedic culture, to claim a particular status on the basis of one’s family relations was itself indicative of a fallen position. Kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas should be given status according to their merit, by their qualities of work and character. When the caste system in India became degraded, people proudly claimed to be relatives of kṣatriyas or brāhmaṇas, though in the past such a claim, unaccompanied by tangible qualifications, indicated a fallen position.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As for ourselves, O tiger among men, we belong to a family of fallen kṣatriyas, descendants of King Ikṣvāku. My name is Mucukunda, my Lord, and I am the son of Yauvanāśva.
    Commentary

    Though he had indicated his own position, he noted Krsna’s silence. Therefore he decided to introduce himself, noting his own good qualifications. By saying he was a low class ksatriya, he intended to show his humility, and thus his good quality.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    What is the ability of a fallen soul to inquire about the birth of an exalted person? And how can this be told to a fallen person? Therefore I should tell about my birth and history in order to surrender to him. He then tells about himself. Mucukunda acts in this way as part of Kṛṣṇa’s human pastimes. Thinking himself fallen, he uses the word tu (but) to indicate that speaking of himself is a different topic. I belong to the family of Ikṣvāku. He calls himself a fallen kṣatriya (kṣatra-bandhavaḥ) out of humility. Yuvanāśva’s son was Māndhātā Mucukunda does not utter his father’s name out of respect. Mucukunda was his son. O tiger among men! Though I am the best of men since I descend from Ikṣvaku, you are the most excellent. O Lord, with special powers (prabho)!

    We belong to a family of fallen kṣatriyas, descendants of Ikṣvāku — my name is Mucukunda, son of Yauvanāśva. Humble self-introduction names the family's fall along with its lineage; honesty about decline doesn't disqualify devotion.

    Important Words
    • cira-prajāgara — long staying awake
      Compound: cira (long) + prajāgara (staying awake). The yugas of demigod-service. Mucukunda explains his sleep not as laziness but as a body's response to extended dharma-duty. Even his sleep was sevā's consequence.
    • nidrayā — by sleep
      Same word, third occurrence in the chapter (verses 21, 32). The Bhāgavata weights nidrā as the demigod-boon that prepared him for darśana. Gauḍīyas read it as kṛṣṇa-prasāda mediated through devas.
    • vijane — in a solitary place
      Locative — alone, secluded. The Vaiṣṇava ideal of viviktasvāna (Gītā 13.10) is anticipated. But Mucukunda's solitude was preparation; Bhagavān has now joined him, and the verse 61 'wander at will' will replace it.
    • apahata-indriyaḥ — with senses overwhelmed
      Compound: apahata (struck down) + indriyaḥ (senses). His senses were 'struck down' by sleep — the same vocabulary the chapter will use, inverted, for the six enemies (ari-ṣaṭ) in verse 57. The senses sleep here; there they will be put to rest by Bhagavān.
    • utthāpitaḥ — awakened
      Past participle of ut-√sthā, causative. Someone caused him to rise. Mucukunda has not yet realized that the deeper waking — into bhakti — is the one Kṛṣṇa is now causing.
    I was fatigued after remaining awake for a long time, and my senses were overwhelmed by sleep. Thus I slept comfortably here in this solitary place until, just now, someone woke me.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I was fatigued after remaining awake for a long time, and my senses were overwhelmed by sleep. Thus I slept comfortably here in this solitary place until, just now, someone woke me.
    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Having told his name and birth, he hides his inner feelings and tells of the external cause of his sleep and his actions. He does not mention the cause of his staying awake for so long out of humility. My senses were oppressed by sleep. I slept nicely (kāmam), not for personal enjoyment. Until now, there was no disturbance to my sleep.

    Personal Guidance
    I was fatigued after remaining awake for a long time; senses overwhelmed by sleep, I slept comfortably until just now. Long service ends in long sleep; the body's tiredness is acknowledged plainly.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you push past fatigue without honoring its scripture-warranted place?
    • What would 'I am tired' look like as legitimate spiritual speech?
    Analogy

    A traveler explaining how he came to be in this corner of the forest — 'I was tired, I slept; somebody woke me.' The asura's last act, in retrospect, becomes the door through which Kṛṣṇa entered Mucukunda's life.

    Important Words
    • bhasmī-kṛtaḥ — turned to ashes
      Compound: bhasma + kṛtaḥ. Fourth use of bhasma-related vocabulary in the chapter — 12, 22, 50, here. The Bhāgavata pins the chapter together with this word; Kālayavana's combustion is the structural pivot.
    • ātmīyena — by his own
      Adjective from ātman + īya — pertaining to his own self. Mucukunda diagnoses correctly: the asura's pāpa was 'his own' — not the sage's wrath. Bhakta's discernment: see whose karma is at work.
    • pāpmanā — by sinful karma
      Instrumental of pāpman — sin-quality. The cause is named: pāpa, not tapas. Gauḍīyas note: a tapasvī's glance does not, of itself, burn — the asura's accumulated aśubha (verse 8) is the actual fuel.
    • śrīmān — glorious, possessed of śrī
      From śrī. He whom Lakṣmī accompanies. Mucukunda's first epithet for Kṛṣṇa post-darśana names the inseparability of Bhagavān and śrī — the Vaiṣṇava theological commitment that Lakṣmī never leaves Viṣṇu's side.
    • amitra-śāsanaḥ — the chastiser of enemies
      Compound: amitra (non-friend, enemy) + śāsanaḥ (the one who disciplines). Bhagavān's executive aspect. Even before Mucukunda calls Him Nārāyaṇa, he calls Him the punisher of asuras — true to his kṣatriya idiom.
    The man who woke me was burned to ashes by the reaction of his sins. Just then I saw You, possessing a glorious appearance and the power to chastise Your enemies.
    Purport

    Kālayavana had declared himself the enemy of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Yadu dynasty. Through Mucukunda, Śrī Kṛṣṇa destroyed the opposition of that foolish barbarian.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The man who woke me was burned to ashes by the reaction of his sins. Just then I saw You, possessing a glorious appearance and the power to chastise Your enemies.
    Commentary

    I see you the punisher of enemies. Through me you had your enemy Kalayavana killed.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nūnam indicates conjecture. He was turned to ashes by his own sins. Thus his offense was removed. This indicates Mucukunda’s humility. Because his offense was removed he attained great fortune. Sometimes śrīman is seen instead of śrīmān. You killed or punished your enemy here by your intelligence (amitra-śāsanaḥ). Another version has amitra-śātanaḥ with the same meaning.

    Personal Guidance
    The man who woke me was burnt to ashes by his own sins' reaction; then I saw You, glorious and capable of chastising enemies. Karma can wake one person and burn another; the same alarm has different effects.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where does the same event you experience as awakening burn another's life — and what does that reveal?
    • How do you steward your karma so that interruptions become alarms, not ashes?
    Analogy

    Mucukunda summarizes the moment: one man was burned away by his own karma, and immediately, in the same gaze, You appeared. He recognizes the sequence — Bhagavān often follows on the heels of the asura's combustion. The cave was emptied for Him.

    Important Words
    • tejasā — by the effulgence
      Instrumental of tejas. The same tejas that Mucukunda guessed at in verse 28 (tejasvinām tejaḥ) is now experienced as overwhelming. Word-reuse marks the shift from speculation to direct experience.
    • aviṣahyeṇa — unbearable
      From a (not) + vi-sah (bear). The kṣatriya who burned an asura with a glance now confesses he cannot bear Bhagavān's mere effulgence. The hierarchy is established by the bhakta himself.
    • hata-ojasā — with diminished power
      Compound: hata (struck) + ojasā (with vital strength). The very tapas-charged faculties that burned Kālayavana are now 'hata' before Bhagavān's tejas. Confession of relative-impotence is a bhakti-mūla.
    • mahā-bhaga — O most opulent one
      Compound: mahā + bhaga (the six opulences of Bhagavān — bhaga-vān). Mucukunda is now invoking the very root that Bhagavān is named for. The next chapter will see him pronounce 'bhagavān' outright; the vocative is sliding toward it.
    • mānanīyaḥ — to be honored
      Future passive participle of √man — the one whom all embodied beings should honor. The verse's universalizing turn: it is not just Mucukunda; this Person is the proper object of dehinām (embodied beings everywhere) — anticipating Gītā 18.66.
    Your unbearably brilliant effulgence overwhelms our strength, and thus we cannot fix our gaze upon You. O exalted one, You are to be honored by all embodied beings.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Your unbearably brilliant effulgence overwhelms our strength, and thus we cannot fix our gaze upon You. O exalted one, You are to be honored by all embodied beings.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Since our strength is defeated by your power, we cannot ask many questions (praṣṭum) such as “Why have you come here? Where will you go? What are you doing at this moment?” Another version has draṣṭum. Since we cannot even see you, what is the question of speaking and asking questions? Therefore brāhmaṇas and others respect you. That is befitting. O person with greatness more than all other great persons (mahā-bhāga)! The form bhāga from bhaga here indicates “one who personifies all good qualities.”

    Your unbearable effulgence overwhelms our strength; we cannot fix our gaze on You. You are to be honored by all embodied beings. Sometimes vision of the Lord is so bright we must look away; honor compensates for inability to gaze.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where could explicit honoring substitute when you can't 'see' Him directly?
    • What in your devotional discipline functions when vision fails?
    Analogy

    Important Words
    • bhūta-bhāvanaḥ — the origin of all creation
      Compound: bhūta (beings) + bhāvanaḥ (the originator, the one who brings into being). One of Bhagavān's standard names (Gītā 9.5, 10.15). Gauḍīyas read this name as the personalist counterweight to Advaitin 'unmanifest source' — bhāvana is an active, willing Person, not a substrate.
    • prahasan — smiling broadly
      Present participle of pra-√has. Bhagavān's smile precedes His teaching, just as it does in Gītā 2.10 (prahasan iva). Vaiṣṇavas read this smile as the Lord's signature mood when about to disclose Himself.
    • vāṇyā — with words
      Instrumental of vāṇī — speech. The Bhāgavata's whole theological tradition is downstream of Bhagavān's vāṇī — Gītā, Uddhava-gītā, this chapter. Vāṇī is not metaphor; it is mediated revelation.
    • megha-nāda-gabhīrayā — deep as the rumbling of clouds
      Compound: megha (cloud) + nāda (sound) + gabhīrayā (deep). The same ghana-vocabulary that named Kṛṣṇa's complexion (verse 23) now names His voice. The image-cluster is consistent: Bhagavān as the dark-blue, deep-voiced thunder-cloud — Vraja's image, in cave-light.
    [Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued:] Thus addressed by the King, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, origin of all creation, smiled and then replied to him in a voice as deep as the rumbling of clouds.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued:] Thus addressed by the King, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, origin of all creation, smiled and then replied to him in a voice as deep as the rumbling of clouds.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord is inclined to protect any beings (bhūta-bhāvanaḥ) what to speak of his devotee Mucukunda. Therefore he spoke with a smile. His voice was deep like rumbling clouds. This indicates a natural quality of the Lord.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord without hiding himself answered with affection for his devotee. Having been addressed skillfully (saṁbhāṣitaḥ), the protector of all jīvas by his nature (bhūta-bhāvanaḥ), manifesting unlimited qualities like affection for his devotee, spoke while smiling, because he was by nature happy or because he was especially pleased. He spoke with a deep voice as part of his nature or because of special joy at that time, or to show that he was Viṣṇu. Mucunda says tathāhi sajalāmboda-nāda-dhīrataraṁ tava vākyam: your voice is deep like the sound of a rain cloud. Visṇu Purāṇa

    Important Words
    • janma — births
      Same word Mucukunda used at verse 30. The Bhāgavata reuses the bhakta's vocabulary in the Lord's mouth — Kṛṣṇa answers in exactly the terms asked. Vaiṣṇava theology of janma: the Lord's births are countless, divya, and never product of karma.
    • abhidhānāni — names
      From abhi-√dhā — to name, designate. Bhagavān's names are infinite; Gauḍīyas treasure this verse as scriptural ground for nāma-saṅkīrtana. Each name is a doorway; there are thousands; even He cannot enumerate them.
    • sahasraśaḥ — by the thousands
      Adverb — 'thousand-fold-ly.' The number-language of Vaiṣṇava theology refuses to commit to a finite count. Bhagavān is sa-hasra in every dimension — births, names, līlās, devotees.
    • anantatvāt — because of having no limit
      Ablative of anantatva — endlessness. The reason Kṛṣṇa cannot count Himself: He is ananta. Ananta-deva is His own bed (Śeṣa); ananta is His attribute; both poetic and metaphysical.
    • mayā — by Me
      Phrase — 'even by Me, indeed.' The 'even Me' is the chapter's most arresting note: Bhagavān's confession of unbounded Self-extension. Gauḍīyas read this as Kṛṣṇa's own modesty inside His own infinity.
    The Supreme Lord said: My dear friend, I have taken thousands of births, lived thousands of lives and accepted thousands of names. In fact My births, activities and names are limitless, and thus even I cannot count them.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Lord said: My dear friend, I have taken thousands of births, lived thousands of lives and accepted thousands of names. In fact My births, activities and names are limitless, and thus even I cannot count them.
    Commentary

    ‘Though Mucukunda is completely without pride, he showed his position in order to hear my words. Therefore I also, though completely without pride, will now pronounce my own superior position to him. I have said, accordingly as they worship me, I also worship them" Considering this statement, Krsna then spoke.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    My births and activities cannot be counted to even an amount similar to their actual number. Anu can mean similarity according to Viśva. Hi means “for certain.”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord addresses him with respect (aṅga). My births and activities cannot be counted to even an amount similar to their actual number. Anu can mean similarity according to Viśva. Hi means “for certain.” “If you cannot count them, you cannot be said to have all powers.” The number is unlimited. The knowledge of the omniscient person is not contradicted by not knowing a flower in the sky.

    I have taken thousands of births, lived thousands of lives, accepted thousands of names; My births, activities and names are limitless. Even He cannot count them. The Lord's biography exceeds the Lord's own bookkeeping.

    Important Words
    • rajāṁsi — dust particles
      Plural of rajas — dust. The homely word for the universe's countable surface. The Bhāgavata loves earthy analogies; Bhagavān's qualities exceed even the earth's dust-count.
    • pārthivāni — earthly
      From pṛthivī — earth. The adjective specifies dust-of-earth, not abstract particles. Earth itself is a Bhagavān-product (avara prakṛti, Gītā 7.4); Kṛṣṇa's qualities exceed His own creation's surface.
    • uru-janmabhiḥ — in many lifetimes
      Compound: uru (many) + janmabhiḥ (with births). Even cosmic-scale effort, over many janmas, cannot enumerate Him. Gauḍīyas read this against impersonalist 'one-life-to-merger' claims — the bhakta has eternally many janmas, all in His service.
    • guṇa — qualities
      Bhagavān's transcendental attributes — sat-cit-ānanda and the unlimited rasa-bearing qualities the Bhāgavatam catalogues. Gauḍīyas distinguish Bhagavān's guṇas (eternally transcendental) from prakṛti's guṇas (sattva-rajas-tamas, conditioning).
    • karhicit — ever
      Particle — 'at any time.' The temporal locator of the impossibility. Not 'rarely' but 'never.' Vaiṣṇava theology's confidence: counting Bhagavān is not a difficult task, it is the kind of task that does not finish.
    After many lifetimes someone might count the dust particles on the earth, but no one can ever finish counting My qualities, activities, names and births.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After many lifetimes someone might count the dust particles on the earth, but no one can ever finish counting My qualities, activities, names and births.
    Commentary

    Someone has at some time counted (vimame) all the particles of dust on the earth.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Vimame should be vimami. One may count the particles of dust, but not my births which have names according to my qualities and activities. Śrīdhara Svāmī says that janmāṇi in this verse also indicates “activities” since this is referred to in the next verse.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Vimame should be vimami. Though his qualities were not in question, in this verse he explains that his qualities like his activities are unlimited. One may count the particles of dust, but not my births which have names according to my qualities and activities.

    Important Words
    • kāla-traya — the three phases of time
      Compound: kāla + traya (triplet). Past, present, future. Bhagavān's janma-karma is co-extensive with all of time, because (verse 19) He is Time. Vaiṣṇava metaphysics: the avatāra's life happens in time, but His person stands outside it.
    • upapannāni — occurring
      Past participle of upa-√pad — to fall to, occur. Bhagavān's deeds 'fall to' all three times — they have happened, are happening, will happen. The avatāras are not single-event; they are cyclic and continual.
    • parama-ṛṣayaḥ — the greatest sages
      Compound: parama (greatest) + ṛṣayaḥ (sages). Vyāsa, Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, Śuka. Even these cannot reach the end. Gauḍīyas read this as the structural reason for the Bhāgavata being twelve cantos rather than complete — paramparā never finishes.
    • anukramantaḥ — enumerating
      Present participle of anu-√kram — to step after, enumerate one-by-one. The same root as Anu-kramaṇī (the indices that summarize Vedic texts). Even the great enumerators are inadequate to Bhagavān.
    • antam — the end
      From anta. There is no antam. The bhakti-attitude embraces this; the speculator wearies of it. Gauḍīyas read endlessness not as frustration but as the structural ground of perpetual rasa.
    O King, the greatest sages enumerate My births and activities, which take place throughout the three phases of time, but never do they reach the end of them.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O King, the greatest sages enumerate My births and activities, which take place throughout the three phases of time, but never do they reach the end of them.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The greatest sages, even knowers of Vedānta, successively cannot count my births and activities, birth, names and qualities which appear in past, present and future. Yato vāco nivartante: the Lord cannot be fully described by words. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad)

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The sages count my birth and activities taking place in past, present and future and cannot reach an end. The qualities are even more. Guṇātmanas te’ pi guṇān vimātum: it is impossible to count the qualities of you who are composed of all qualities. (SB 10.14.7) Since the names arise from the qualities and activities they are also unlimited. The births are unlimited because the Lord appears many times over time and there are various forms which are many. The extent of time is unlimited. Counting in order, the great sages like Bhṛgu find that there is no end. O king! You can understand this since many great sages have gathered here because of your being a great king.

    Personal Guidance
    The greatest sages enumerate My births and activities through all three phases of time but never reach the end. Even the sages don't finish — the joy is in the inquiry itself, not in completion.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you want closure on what is designed to remain open?
    • Could you take joy in the inquiry itself rather than waiting for the end?
    Analogy

    The greatest sages enumerate Bhagavān's birth and deeds across past, present and future — and still do not reach the end. The Bhāgavata is itself an instance of this enumeration; it confesses, mid-recital, its own incompletability. A holy text that knows it cannot end is a Vaiṣṇava text.

    Important Words
    • viriñcena — by Lord Brahmā
      Instrumental of Viriñca — Brahmā. The four-faced demiurge of this universe, but explicitly a creature in Bhāgavatam — he prays to Viṣṇu in SB 10.1. Gauḍīyas firmly subordinate Brahmā to Bhagavān; this verse cites that subordination.
    • dharma-guptaye — for the protection of religious principles
      Compound: dharma + guptaye (for the guarding). Echoes Gītā 4.7-8 directly — paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām, dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya. The Bhāgavata and Gītā speak with one voice on the avatāra's purpose.
    • ānakadundubheḥ — of Vasudeva (Ānakadundubhi)
      Genitive — at whose birth the kettle-drums (ānaka-dundubhi) of heaven sounded; hence Vasudeva's epithet. Even the father's name carries the celebratory acoustic of Bhagavān's descent.
    • vāsudevaḥ iti — by the name Vāsudeva
      Phrase — 'by the name Vāsudeva.' Bhagavān names Himself. Gauḍīyas note: in the Pāñcarātra system, Vāsudeva is the first of the catur-vyūha (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha). The name He gives Mucukunda is the head of His own emanation-tree.
    • yadu-kule — in the Yadu dynasty
      Same compound as verse 8 — the lineage Kālayavana wielded as a taunt is here re-claimed by Kṛṣṇa as His own celebrated home. The taunt becomes the answer.
    • avatīrṇaḥ — descended
      Past participle of ava-√tṝ — to cross down. The technical Vaiṣṇava term for divine descent. Avatāra is not 'incarnation' in the Western sense; it is Bhagavān's own self-deposition into the world without loss of Self.
    Nonetheless, O friend, I will tell you about My current birth, name and activities. Kindly hear. Some time ago, Lord Brahmā requested Me to protect religious principles and destroy the demons who were burdening the earth. Thus I descended in the Yadu dynasty, in the home of Ānakadundubhi. Indeed, because I am the son of Vasudeva, people call Me Vāsudeva.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Nonetheless, O friend, I will tell you about My current birth, name and activities. Kindly hear. Some time ago, Lord Brahmā requested Me to protect religious principles and destroy the demons who were burdening the earth. Thus I descended in the Yadu dynasty, in the home of Ānakadundubhi. Indeed, because I am the son of Vasudeva, people call Me Vāsudeva.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    However, on your request, hear from me as I speak about my present birth and activities, though they are difficult to understand. Hear only, but do not desire to understand in truth or to a great degree. I was requested previously to protect the devotees (dharma-guptaye) and destroy the demons. I have now appeared in the Yadu dynasty. “As Vāsudeva, your name was previously famous as he in whom all beings reside (vasanti yatra bhūtāni), taking the name as an ordinary compound. But this name appears to be recent because of special qualities which had previously been hidden.” I am famous as the son of Vasudeva. I am most famous (hi) among all the forms of the Lord who appeared as sons such as Rāma, since I am the main form.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Hear about my present birth from me with attention. I was requested by Brahmā, along with Śiva and Bhūmi, arriving on the bank of the milk ocean according to rules. I should protect dharma in order to protect the devotees. He speaks of his birth first. I appeared, not arising from a womb, as the son of Vasudeva, who was born the sound of drums from heaven. This indicates his fame and greatness. They call me Vāsudeva. “This name already exists. He is the presiding deity of citta.” I am the son of Vasudeva. That is the well-known name at this time. That is me alone. Though it is possible to have that name as a son of Rāma or other avatāras, it is famous as my name, because of affection for my father. Other names like Kṛṣṇa, Dāmodara, Govinda are not mentioned as they are secret. Since he is not qualified to hear about this birth, his identity in the next verse is described. And later, in describing his activities, his pastimes in Gokula are not mentioned, but the description of his killing demons is explained.

    Personal Guidance
    I will tell you about this current birth: Brahmā asked Me to protect religious principles and destroy demons; I descended in the Yadu dynasty. The current incarnation has a specific commission; particular missions are named clearly.
    Reflection Questions
    • Could you name the specific commission of your current life with such clarity?
    • Where do you live as if you had no particular mission?
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa narrows the infinite into a single biography for His friend: 'Brahmā asked, I descended in the Yadu line at Vasudeva's home, people call Me Vāsudeva.' The cosmic confession contracts into a name a friend can use.

    Stories
    Brahmā's prayer that began the avatāra

    At SB 10.1.17-25, Bhūmi-devī comes weeping to the demigods, asuras have crushed the earth's order, and Brahmā leads them all to the milk-ocean to petition Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu's reply — that He will appear in the Yadu line at Vasudeva's home — is the exact promise Kṛṣṇa is now relating to Mucukunda eons later.

    Gauḍīyas treasure this back-reference: the same Bhāgavata-text Mucukunda has not yet read is being summarized to him by its own protagonist. The avatāra remembers, and tells, His own appearance-narrative.

    Important Words
    • kālanemiḥ — the demon Kālanemi
      The previous incarnation of Kaṁsa. Bhāgavatam's view of asuric continuity: demons return until they are released by Bhagavān's direct action. The chapter's whole metaphysics of birth (verses 36-40) is in service of explaining such reincarnations.
    • kaṁsaḥ — Kaṁsa
      Devakī's brother, the central asura of Canto 10. Kṛṣṇa names him by name as a 'past completed action.' The book is recursive — Mucukunda is in the same canto whose protagonists Kṛṣṇa is summarizing.
    • pralamba — Pralamba
      The asura killed by Balarāma (SB 10.18). Mentioning him here folds Balarāma's deeds into Kṛṣṇa's own account — the two are non-different in mission, and Kṛṣṇa speaks for both.
    • sat-dviṣaḥ — envious of the pious
      Compound: sat (the saintly) + dviṣaḥ (haters). The Vaiṣṇava category for asura — not 'evil' abstractly but specifically 'devotee-haters.' Bhagavān's mission targets those who target His devotees.
    • tigma-cakṣuṣā — by the piercing glance
      Compound: tigma (sharp, fiery) + cakṣuṣā (by the eye). Mucukunda's glance is credited inside Bhagavān's own deeds-list. Gauḍīyas treasure this: the bhakta's instrument is the Lord's instrument; Mucukunda's eye-fire is Kṛṣṇa's action accomplished through him.
    I have killed Kālanemi, reborn as Kaṁsa, as well as Pralamba and other enemies of the pious. And now, O King, this barbarian has been burnt to ashes by your piercing glance.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I have killed Kālanemi, reborn as Kaṁsa, as well as Pralamba and other enemies of the pious. And now, O King, this barbarian has been burnt to ashes by your piercing glance.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He describes his activities. Kālameni and Kaṁsa were killed by me.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He describes his activities. Kālameni and Kaṁsa were killed by me because they hated devotees (sad-dviṣaḥ). O king, shining with intelligence (rājan), you can understand this. Or o king shining with the benedictions of the devatās like Śiva! You cannot be killed.

    Related values & verses
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    I have killed Kālanemi reborn as Kaṁsa, Pralamba, and other enemies of the pious; and now this barbarian was burnt by your piercing glance. The Lord credits Mucukunda for the latest deed; collaboration is acknowledged.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you take credit alone for what was collaboration with the Lord?
    • How does Kṛṣṇa's crediting His devotee model your own credit-sharing?
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa lists His current births' work like a soldier reading a brief: Kālanemi reborn as Kaṁsa, Pralamba, others, and now this Yavana — burnt to ash by your glance. He acknowledges Mucukunda's role; the sage's tapas is enrolled into the avatāra's mission.

    Stories
    Kālanemi to Kaṁsa

    Kālanemi was the asura killed by Viṣṇu in an earlier age (referenced in Hari-vaṁśa and the Bhāgavata itself at SB 10.51.41). His soul, untransformed, reincarnated as Kaṁsa — the same enmity, the same Lord, a new birth.

    Gauḍīyas read this as the Vaiṣṇava metaphysics of asura-rebirth: hatred toward Bhagavān is itself a form of remembrance, sustained across lives, until finally consumed by direct contact with His person. Even the demon's bondage to Bhagavān is a kind of bond.

    Important Words
    • anugraha-artham — for the sake of mercy
      Compound: anugraha (favor, grace) + artham (for the sake of). Bhagavān's stated motive is anugraha — not cosmic management, not karmic balance, but personal favor. Gauḍīyas read this as the definition of grace: Bhagavān moves for the devotee's sake.
    • prārthitaḥ — prayed to
      Past participle of pra-√arth — to ask, pray. Mucukunda's prayers are explicitly acknowledged. The Vaiṣṇava confidence: every sincere prayer is heard, recorded, and answered at the right moment.
    • pracuram — abundantly
      Adverb — copiously. Mucukunda prayed not once but extensively. Gauḍīyas teach that the persistence of prayer is itself part of the prayer; the Lord responds to those who do not stop.
    • bhakta-vatsalaḥ — affectionate to devotees
      Compound: bhakta + vatsalaḥ (calf-loving, tender). The Bhāgavata's signature epithet for Bhagavān. Vatsala-vocabulary recalls Yaśodā's tenderness for child-Kṛṣṇa — here turned inside out: Kṛṣṇa is vatsala toward His bhaktas.
    • guhām — the cave
      The cave is now reclassified — not a place of sleep but a place of anugraha. Same physical location, transformed by the visitor. Gauḍīyas read this as bhakti's geography: any place Bhagavān enters becomes Vaikuṇṭha for the devotee there.
    Since in the past you repeatedly prayed to Me, I have personally come to this cave to show you mercy, for I am affectionately inclined to My devotees.
    Purport

    It is apparent from this verse that Mucukunda was a devotee of the Supreme Lord. He had prayed for the Lord’s association, and now Śrī Kṛṣṇa granted his fervent request.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Since in the past you repeatedly prayed to Me, I have personally come to this cave to show you mercy, for I am affectionately inclined to My devotees.
    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I have not come here to kill Kālayavana. That could have been done by other means. I came to give mercy to you. That is expressed in this verse. Though endowed with greatness, I have come here out of compliance. Viśva says that upa can mean compliance. You requested to see me with pure devotion (pra—arthitaḥ) many times (pracuram), because I am affectionate to devotees. Just by showing myself, unlimited desires of devotees are fulfilled and everything is fulfilled by satisfying devotees. Or I came to the cave because I am affectionate to the devotees.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Anahankarah (Freedom from False Ego)Kshama (Forgiveness / Patience)Karuna (Kindness / Compassion)
    Related verses
    BG 15.9 BG 12.13 BG 18.64 BG 2.62 BG 3.11 BG 12.3 SB 4.29.2 BG 9.11 BG 7.8 BG 10.3 BG 13.1 BG 5.18 BG 6.1 BG 6.5 BG 1.1 BG 16.4
    Personal Guidance
    Since in the past you repeatedly prayed to Me, I have personally come to this cave to show you mercy — I am affectionately inclined to devotees. Past prayers have a long memory in the Lord's reckoning; old asks are eventually answered in person.
    Reflection Questions
    • What old prayer of yours might be quietly approaching its visit?
    • How do you keep praying when answers are taking generations?
    Analogy

    A king visiting a long-time petitioner whose past prayers have been on file. Kṛṣṇa names His motive: bhakta-vatsalatā — affection for His devotees. The visit is not strategic; it is the heart's debt being paid.

    Stories
    Bhakta-vatsalya across the Bhāgavata

    The same motive — bhakta-vatsalya — moves Bhagavān to come for Gajendra (SB 8.3), for Prahlāda (SB 7.8), for Dhruva (SB 4.9), for Ambarīṣa (SB 9.4). The Bhāgavata's structural claim is that none of these visits is coincidental; each was earned by a devotee's prior prayer, and each is honored at the appointed moment.

    Mucukunda's case is paradigm: he prayed in past ages (prārthitaḥ pracuram pūrvam tvayā); Kṛṣṇa names that prayer here, in the cave. The bhakti record is exact, and the Lord's coming is its mathematics.

    Important Words
    • varān — benedictions
      Same word as verse 20. The demigods offered varas but withheld kaivalya; Kṛṣṇa offers varas with no withholding. The contrast between deva-vara and bhagavān-vara is structural in this chapter.
    • vṛṇīṣva — please choose
      Imperative of √vṛ. The same form the demigods used in verse 20. Bhagavān's offer formally mirrors theirs but exceeds their scope — He can give what they could not.
    • rāja-ṛṣe — O saintly King
      Compound: rāja + ṛṣi — a king who is also a seer. Mucukunda has earned both halves of the title. Gauḍīyas note that the rāja-ṛṣi category (Janaka, Yudhiṣṭhira, Pṛthu, Khaṭvāṅga, Mucukunda) is the Bhāgavata's preferred royal exemplar.
    • prasannaḥ — having satisfied
      Past participle of pra-√sad — to be clear, gracious. The whole bhakti-purpose: making Bhagavān prasanna. From the Lord's side, prasāda flows; from the bhakta's side, prasanna-tā is the goal.
    • śocitum — to lament
      Infinitive of √śuc — to grieve. The same root as 'aśocyān anvaśocas tvam' (Gītā 2.11). The Lord's prasanna-tā ends śoka — material lamentation. The Bhāgavata's promise to every devotee.
    Now choose some benedictions from Me, O saintly King. I will fulfill all your desires. One who has satisfied Me need never again lament.
    Purport

    The ācāryas explain that we lament when we feel incomplete, when we have lost something or when we fail to achieve something desirable. One who has satisfied Kṛṣṇa and thus attained the Lord’s mercy will never be troubled in these ways. Lord Kṛṣṇa is the reservoir of all pleasure, and He enjoys sharing His spiritual bliss with all living beings. We need only cooperate with the Supreme Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Now choose some benedictions from Me, O saintly King. I will fulfill all your desires. One who has satisfied Me need never again lament.
    Commentary

    The person who has satisfied me does not have to lament. The benedictions given by others are perishable, and therefore the benefactor laments when the boon disappears. But for one who surrenders to me, I give benedictions which are not perishable. Therefore he does not lament.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I will fulfill all desires suitable for a king and sage. Those who surrender to me, what to speak of those who are full of devotion will no longer lament. He hints that Mucukunda should not desire any other benediction than surrender.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I will fulfill all desires suitable for a king and sage. Those who surrender to me, what to speak of those who are full of devotion, will no longer lament. Or he who attains the boon will no longer lament. Ask for happiness after this life as well, since you are a sage among kings. You are qualified for happiness in this life and the next since you are a king and a sage.

    Now choose benedictions — I will fulfill all desires; one who has satisfied Me need never lament. Access to the Lord includes invitation to ask; lamentation about the unwanted ends when He is fully pleased.
    Reflection Questions

    • Where could satisfaction of Him replace satisfaction of yourself?

    Important Words
    • praṇamya — after bowing down
      Absolutive of pra-√nam. The physical sign of recognition. Before words, the body bows. Gauḍīyas place praṇāma among the six limbs of śaraṇāgati — the embodied confession that Bhagavān is higher.
    • mudā-anvitaḥ — filled with joy
      Phrase — joy-accompanied. Mucukunda's mood at recognition is mudā — bhakti-ānanda. The Bhāgavata is careful: recognition of Bhagavān produces joy, not fear; joy is the diagnostic affect of right-relation.
    • nārāyaṇam devam — Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord
      Phrase — the highest Vaiṣṇava theological name in this chapter. Nārāyaṇa = nāra (men, waters) + ayana (shelter): the resting-place of all souls. Gauḍīyas read this name's appearance as the moment Mucukunda crosses from kṣatriya-recognition to Vaiṣṇava-recognition.
    • garga-vākyam — the words of Garga
      Compound: garga + vākyam (speech). Paramparā transmission named. Even centuries of sleep cannot erase a guru's words; they wait in the bhakta until Bhagavān's darśana calls them up.
    • anusmaran — remembering
      Present participle of anu-√smṛ — to recall following-along. Smaraṇa, one of the nine limbs of bhakti, is activated. Mucukunda's bhakti begins to function in its proper Gauḍīya form precisely at this verse.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Mucukunda bowed down to the Lord when he heard this. Remembering the words of the sage Garga, he joyfully recognized Kṛṣṇa to be the Supreme Lord, Nārāyaṇa. The King then addressed Him as follows.
    Purport

    Although the Lord here appears as four-handed Nārāyaṇa, we may say that Mucukunda was addressing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. All of this is taking place within the context of kṛṣṇa-līlā, the pastimes of Lord Kṛṣṇa. It is well known to Vaiṣṇavas that the four-handed forms of Viṣṇu, or Nārāyaṇa, are expansions of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Thus within the pastimes of Lord Kṛṣṇa there may also appear viṣṇu-līlā, the activities of Viṣṇu. Such are the qualities and activities of the Supreme Godhead. Deeds that for us would be extraordinary and even impossible are commonplace, effortless pastimes for the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī informs us that Mucukunda was aware of the prediction of the ancient sage Garga that in the twenty-eighth millennium the Supreme Lord would descend. According to Ācārya Viśvanātha, Garga Muni further informed Mucukunda that he would personally see the Lord. Now it was all happening.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Mucukunda bowed down to the Lord when he heard this. Remembering the words of the sage Garga, he joyfully recognized Kṛṣṇa to be the Supreme Lord, Nārāyaṇa. The King then addressed Him as follows.
    Commentary

    Remembering the words of Garga, "In the twenty eighth yuga Krsna will appear and become visible to you." Mucukunda recognized Krsna, bowed to him, and spoke.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Remembering Garga’s words, recognizing that Nārāyaṇa was Svayam Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa, in joy he offered respects and spoke.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Remembering Garga’s words, recognizing that Nārāyaṇa was Svayam Bhagavān, Kṛṣṇa, in joy he offered respects and spoke. Devam means he shone brightly.

    Personal Guidance
    Mucukunda bows, remembers Garga's words, and joyfully recognizes Kṛṣṇa as Nārāyaṇa. Memory of an earlier sage's prophecy enables present recognition; preparation in the past meets revelation in the present.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which earlier teaching prepares you to recognize what Kṛṣṇa shows you today?
    • What 'Garga's words' from your tradition could you bring back into active memory?
    Analogy

    Mucukunda bows, and an old memory surfaces: the sage Garga had told him of the Yadu-avatāra. Recognition is recall — what the guru placed in him eons ago now flowers in the cave. Bhakti's pedagogy: store paramparā-teaching, trust that it will ripen when needed.

    Stories
    Garga's name-giving

    Earlier in this very canto (SB 10.8.13-19), Gargācārya, the family guru of the Yadus, performed Kṛṣṇa's name-giving ceremony in Nanda's home, declared Him to be Nārāyaṇa Himself, and listed His future deeds. The same Garga had, eons earlier, given Mucukunda the doctrine of the Yadu-avatāra; that teaching now flowers.

    Gauḍīyas read this as the Bhāgavata's structural argument for paramparā: the same ācārya teaches across yugas, threading bhaktas to bhaktas, recognition to recognition. Mucukunda remembers Garga; we remember through our own paramparā-line.

    Important Words
    • vimohitaḥ — bewildered
      Past participle of vi-√muh — thoroughly deluded. The bhakta names the universal condition before exempting himself. Gauḍīyas read vimoha as māyā's signature effect — not stupidity, but misdirected longing.
    • māyayā-tvadīyayā — by Your own illusory energy
      Phrase — māyā belongs to Bhagavān. Acintya-bhedābheda's exact point: māyā is Kṛṣṇa's energy, not a rival principle. It veils only those who turn away; the surrendered are crossed over (Gītā 7.14). Mucukunda is naming the very source he is escaping.
    • anartha-dṛk — one who does not see his real benefit
      Compound: an (not) + artha (true benefit) + dṛk (seer). Bhāgavatam's classic diagnostic. The materialist is not lazy but mis-seeing; he genuinely pursues what he thinks is artha. Vaiṣṇavas teach that bhagavad-bhakti alone is the real artha.
    • duḥkha-prabhaveṣu — in things that cause misery
      Compound: duḥkha (misery) + prabhaveṣu (sources). Family-affairs are duḥkha-source even when pleasant — the Bhāgavata's unflinching diagnosis. Gauḍīyas treasure that bhakti is the only sukha-source not collapsing into duḥkha.
    • vañcitaḥ — cheated
      Past participle of √vañc — to deceive. The universal jīva is vañcita — cheated of its real position. Vaiṣṇava theology never blames māyā morally; it names the jīva's choice to face away. But its consequence is being vañcita.
    Śrī Mucukunda said: O Lord, the people of this world, both men and women, are bewildered by Your illusory energy. Unaware of their real benefit, they do not worship You but instead seek happiness by entangling themselves in family affairs, which are actually sources of misery.
    Purport

    Mucukunda immediately makes it clear that he is not going to ask the Lord for material blessings. He has advanced, spiritually, far beyond those who try to exploit religion for all kinds of material benefits. Artha means “value,” and the negation of this word, anartha, means “that which is valueless or useless.” Thus the term anartha-dṛk indicates those whose vision is focused on valueless things, who have not understood what actual artha, or value, is. All that glitters is not gold, and Mucukunda here emphatically states that we should not ruin our spiritual chances by entangling ourselves in the fool’s gold of bodily relationships. We are meant to love the Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śrī Mucukunda said: O Lord, the people of this world, both men and women, are bewildered by Your illusory energy. Unaware of their real benefit, they do not worship You but instead seek happiness by entangling themselves in family affairs, which are actually sources of misery.
    Commentary

    That a person rejects devotion to you and instead accepts objects of lust is your maya. That is expressed in this verse. Both men and women, bewildered by your maya, become cheated, and engage in family life.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Because this māyā belongs to you (tvadīyayā) it is difficult to overcome. This person (ayam janaḥ) who can be directly seen does not worship you. He is attached to his houses and related objects and, though he experiences direct grief, he never becomes detached. He is cheated by lust and other factors.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O supreme Lord! Because this māyā belongs to you (tvadīyayā), it is difficult to overcome. Therefore I am especially bewildered. This person (ayam janaḥ) who can be directly seen, or this person among all jīvas, does not worship you. He is attached to his houses and related objects and, though he experiences direct grief, he never becomes detached. He is cheated by lust and other factors. Or a person like me (ayam janaḥ) born in a good family, not identifying with the body by detachment, is completely bewildered. Both men and women have material vision (anartha-dṛk). This person is cheated, by women and house etc.

    Personal Guidance
    O Lord, the people of this world, men and women, are bewildered by Your illusory energy; not knowing their real benefit, they don't worship You but seek happiness in family affairs — actually sources of misery. The wise diagnosis precedes the wise request.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you seek happiness in arrangements that are diagnosable as sources of misery?
    • What honest diagnosis would precede a wise petition?
    Analogy

    Mucukunda's stuti opens with diagnosis: men and women, bewildered by Your māyā, look for happiness in family entanglement — which is itself the source of their misery. The bhakta's clear-eyed survey of saṁsāra; only after diagnosing it can he renounce it.

    Important Words
    • durlabham — rarely obtained
      From dur (difficult) + √labh — hard to attain. Human birth is durlabha — Bhāgavatam's standard refrain (cf. SB 11.9.29, 11.20.17). Gauḍīyas read this as Bhagavān's gift of opportunity; squandering it is the deepest tragedy.
    • mānuṣam — the human form
      From manu — descended from Manu, possessing intelligence (manas). The body capable of bhakti-sādhana. Animals cannot perform sādhana-bhakti; humans can. The verse's whole rhetorical force depends on this asymmetry.
    • pāda-aravindam — lotus feet
      Compound: pāda + aravindam (lotus). The first object of Vaiṣṇava worship. Mucukunda's verse 27 noticed those feet; now he urges all humans to worship them. The image runs through the whole chapter.
    • asat-matiḥ — of impure mentality
      Compound: asat (impure, unreal) + matiḥ (intellect). The diagnostic — not 'evil heart' but 'wrong-pointing intellect.' Buddhi turned to asat rather than sat. The fix is to redirect, not to repress.
    • gṛha-andha-kūpe — in the blind well of home
      Compound: gṛha (home) + andha (blind) + kūpe (well). The vivid Bhāgavata image — household as andha-kūpa. Not 'home is evil,' but 'home-as-blind-well is evil' — clinging to it as ultimate is the fall. Gauḍīyas live in homes; they do not live for them.
    That person has an impure mind who, despite having somehow or other automatically obtained the rare and highly evolved human form of life, does not worship Your lotus feet. Like an animal that has fallen into a blind well, such a person has fallen into the darkness of a material home.
    Purport

    Our real home is in the kingdom of God. Despite our tenacious determination to remain in our material home, death will rudely eject us from the theater of material affairs. To stay at home is not bad, nor is it bad to devote ourselves to our loved ones. But we must understand that our real home is eternal, in the spiritual kingdom. The word ayatnataḥ indicates that human life has been automatically awarded to us. We have not constructed our human bodies, and therefore we should not foolishly claim, “This body is mine.” The human form is a gift of God and should be used to achieve the perfection of God consciousness. One who does not understand this is asan-mati, possessed of dull, mundane understanding.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    That person has an impure mind who, despite having somehow or other automatically obtained the rare and highly evolved human form of life, does not worship Your lotus feet. Like an animal that has fallen into a blind well, such a person has fallen into the darkness of a material home.
    Commentary

    The ignorant man, for a few pennies sells the cintamani jewel. That is the essence of this verse. After attaining a rare human birth in the land of Bharata (iha) with no deformity, falling into the well of household life like an animal, the materialist fails to worship you.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Mānuṣaṁ should be mānuṣyam (human form of life). O Lord who destroys all suffering (anagha) for the person worships you a little! By karma (kathaṣcit), having attained a human form, he does not worship lotus feet. He does not mention “your” feet since it is understood from the context. He does not worship with reverence or inattentively. This is because he is without discrimination (asan-matiḥ) like an animal. Thus he falls into the dark well of household life.

    Personal Guidance
    Impure-minded is one who, having obtained the rare human form, doesn't worship Your feet — like an animal fallen into a blind well. Time will rudely eject us from our material 'homes'; only worship makes that ejection meaningful.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where are you treating the human form as a routine starting point rather than a rare attainment?
    • What worship would render the inevitable ejection a graduation?
    Analogy

    An animal falling into a blind well — once down, it cannot climb out. So is the person who, having received human birth (the rare ascent), still does not worship Bhagavān's lotus feet. The verse's force: human birth is the ladder; refusing to climb is the fall.
